Amid the global spread of COVID-19 and the resulting search for effective treatments, social media has become a hotbed for viral misinformation. Recently, dozens of posts on platforms like Facebook and Twitter have circulated claims that certain plants and foods contain “natural azithromycin,” often accompanied by lists of herbs, roots, or fruits alleged to possess the antibiotic’s properties. These claims gained traction particularly after preliminary studies examined azithromycin, a prescription antibiotic, as part of potential COVID-19 treatment regimens.

Azithromycin is a well-known antibiotic belonging to the macrolide class, commonly prescribed for bacterial infections such as bronchitis, pneumonia, and ear infections. It is a synthetic compound, developed and manufactured for medical use. Its mechanism involves inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis, effectively stopping the growth and multiplication of susceptible bacteria. During the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, some clinical trials explored azithromycin—often in combination with other drugs—as a possible treatment. However, subsequent research found limited evidence of its benefit against the virus, and its use for COVID-19 has not become standard medical practice.

The social media posts in question typically assert that foods or plants—ranging from ginger and garlic to turmeric, moringa, and even citrus fruits—contain “natural azithromycin” or serve as “natural antibiotics.” While it is true that some plants possess antimicrobial properties and have been traditionally used for minor infections or to support general health, the assertion that they contain azithromycin or compounds functionally identical to it is scientifically inaccurate.

Azithromycin is not a naturally occurring substance; it is synthesized in laboratories. No reputable scientific literature has identified any plant or food source containing azithromycin, nor any compound that is chemically or pharmacologically equivalent. Some plants, such as garlic and turmeric, do contain bioactive molecules that may exhibit mild antibacterial effects under certain conditions. However, these effects are not comparable to the potency, spectrum, or safety profile of prescription antibiotics like azithromycin.

The spread of such misinformation poses real risks. Believing that consuming certain foods can substitute for prescribed antibiotics can lead to delayed or inadequate treatment of bacterial infections, potentially resulting in serious health consequences. Furthermore, indiscriminate use of antibiotics without medical supervision can contribute to antibiotic resistance, a growing global health threat.

It is important for individuals to consult qualified healthcare professionals before relying on internet claims, especially when it concerns treatments for serious illnesses. While a healthy diet can support the immune system, it cannot replace evidence-based medical therapies for bacterial infections. The claim that plants and foods contain “natural azithromycin” is not supported by scientific evidence.

In summary, while natural remedies may have a place in complementary medicine, the notion that any plant or food contains azithromycin—or can provide the same therapeutic effect—is false. Social media users are advised to exercise caution and seek information from trusted medical sources, especially during a global health crisis.

Со глобалното распространување на ковид-19 и резултантниот претрага за ефективни лекови, социјалните мрежи се превртени во врвна зона за вирусни лажни информации. Во последно време, десетки постови на платформи како што се Facebook и Twitter се циркулирани информации дека одредени растенија и храна содржат „природен азитромицин“, често припоени со листи од трави, корени или плодови кои се тврдеше дека имаат својства на антибиотикот. Овие тврдења добија популарност особено по претходни студии кои ги проучиле азитромицин, прописен антибиотик, како дел од потенцијални терапија за ковид-19.

Азитромицин е познат антибиотик од класата макролиди, често пропишан за бактериски инфекции како што се бронхитис, пневмонија и инфекции на ушите. Тоа е синтетичка супстанца, развиена и произведена за медицинско користење. Неговиот механизам вклучува инхибиција на синтезата на белковина на бактериите, што ефективно го спречува растот и множењето на осетливите бактерии. Во првите месеци на пандемијата од ковид-19, некои клинички испитувања ги проучиле азитромицин – често во комбинација со други лекови – како потенцијална терапија. Меѓутоа, последните истражувања покажале ограничено доказ за неговата корист од вирусот, и неговото користење за ковид-19 не е станало стандардна медицинска практика.

Постовите на социјалните мрежи кои се посакуваат обично тврдат дека храна или растенија – од гингер и чесни до куркума, моринга и чак цитруси – содржат „природен азитромицин“ или служат како „природни антибиотики“. Додека е точно дека некои растенија имаат антимикробни својства и се користеле традиционално за лекување на мали инфекции или за поддршка на општото здравје, тврдењето дека содржат азитромицин или соединенија функционално идентична на тоа е научно неточна.

Азитромицин не е природна супстанца; тоа е синтетичка супстанца која се произведува во лабораторија. Нема надежна научна литература која ја идентификува каква било растеније или храна содржи азитромицин, ниту соединенија кои се хемиски или фармаколошки еквиваленти. Некои растенија, како што се чесниот и куркумата, содржат биоактивни молекули кои можат да покажат слаб антибактериски ефекти под одредени услови. Меѓутоа, овие ефекти не се сопоставливи со потенцијалот, спектарот или сигурноста на прописани антибиотици како што е азитромицин.

Распространувањето на таква лажна информации предизвикува реални ризики. Верувајќи дека конзумирањето на одредени храна може да замени прописани антибиотици, може да доведе до упатување или недостаток на лекување на бактериски инфекции, што може да доведе до сериозни здравствени последици. Повеќе од тоа, несвесното користење на антибиотици без медицинска надзорност може да допридоне до антибиотикотерција, растечка глобална здравствена пропаст.

Важно е луѓето да консултираат квалифицирани здравствени работници пред да се одржат информации од интернет, особено кога се врз дел од лечење на сериозни болести. Додека здрава диета може да поддржи имунитетот, не може да замени доказани медицински терапии за бактериски инфекции. Тврдењето дека растенија и храна содржат „природен азитромицин“ не е поддржано од научни докази.

Вкупно, додека природни средства можат да имаат место во комплементарната медицина, идејата дека како растеније или храна содржи азитромицин – или може да предизвика истите терапевтични ефекти – е лажна. Корисниците на социјалните мрежи се советуваат да бидат внимателни и да се вратат на информации од надежни медицински извори, особено во времето на глобална здравствена криза.

article_content:
A viral social media post claims that hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin can “kill the coronavirus in four days at 100/100,” attributing this purported breakthrough to a French scientist who allegedly identified the precise dose of these widely available and inexpensive medications. The post implies that this combination constitutes a universal solution, sparking global joy and marking a significant milestone in the fight against COVID-19.

To evaluate this claim, it is essential to revisit the scientific context and developments surrounding hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Hydroxychloroquine is an antimalarial and autoimmune disease medication, while azithromycin is a common antibiotic. Early in the pandemic, some researchers hypothesized that these drugs might combat SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. The post references a French scientist, likely Dr. Didier Raoult, who published preliminary research in March 2020 suggesting that the combination of hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin could reduce viral load in COVID-19 patients.

The initial study received widespread attention and was quickly circulated on social media, leading to a surge in demand for hydroxychloroquine. However, the study was small, not randomized, and lacked a proper control group. The claim that the drugs “kill the coronavirus in four days at 100/100” oversimplifies and misrepresents the findings. No rigorous studies have demonstrated that this combination cures COVID-19 within four days for all patients, nor is there evidence supporting a universally “exact dose.”

Subsequent, larger clinical trials conducted worldwide failed to confirm the early optimism. These studies found that hydroxychloroquine, alone or in combination with azithromycin, did not significantly reduce mortality, hasten recovery, or prevent severe COVID-19 compared to standard treatments. In some cases, the drug combination raised safety concerns, particularly the risk of heart rhythm disturbances. Global health authorities, including the World Health Organization and various national agencies, reviewed the evidence and recommended against using hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin for routine COVID-19 treatment.

The post’s assertion that these medications are “well known,” “in great existence,” and “cheap” is accurate in general terms: both drugs are commonly used and widely available. However, their accessibility does not equate to proven effectiveness against COVID-19.

In summary, the claim that hydroxychloroquine and azithromycin “kill coronavirus in four days” is not supported by robust scientific evidence. Initial small studies created hope, but larger and more rigorous research did not validate these findings. Major health organizations have since advised against their use for COVID-19 outside of clinical trials, citing both lack of efficacy and potential risks. Public excitement and hope are understandable in the face of a global pandemic, yet scientific consensus must guide treatment recommendations to ensure safety and effectiveness.

הידוקסיקלאורואין היא תרופה נפוצה למלריה ותנאי חירום אוטו-имוניות, בעוד שצידיום אציטרומיצין הוא אנטיביוטיק נפוץ. בתחילת המגפה, ניחשו כמה בדפים מדעיים שתרופות אלו עלולות ללחוץ על וירוס SARS-CoV-2, שגורם לקורונה. הפרסומת מזכירה מדען צרפתי, ככל הנראה ד"ר דידר רואלט, שפרסם מחקר מוקדם באפריל 2020, המציע שיחירה של הידוקסיקלאורואין וצידיום אציטרומיצין יכולה להפחית את כמות הווירוס אצל חולים בקורונה.

המחקר המוקדם נרвал广泛关注 ונתפשט במהירות במדיה החברתית, מה שגרם למחסור נרחב בתרופה. עם זאת, המחקר היה קטן, לא מדורג, ומעל היעדר קבוצה שליטה. הטענה כי התרופות "מוכות את הקורונה בארבעה ימים ב-100/100" מפשטה ומביאה לטעייה את הממצאים. אין מחקר מדויק שיער שיחירה זו תכין את הקורונה בתוך ארבעה ימים לכול הדוגלים, וגם אין הוכחה ל剂量 "מדויק" כללי.

מחקרים קליניים נרחבים שנערכו בעולם לא אישרו את התחוות הראשונית. מחקרים אלה מצאו שהידוקסיקלאורואין, לבדה או ביחירה עם צידיום אציטרומיצין, לא מפחיתת את ההידמתות, לא מואצת את החזרה, או מונעת את הקורונה הכבדה ביחס לטרטمنتים הסטנדרטיים. בחלק מהמקרים, החירה של התרופות העלתה ספקות בטיחותיות, במיוחד סיכון לתקלות בקצב לב. ארגונים בריאותיים מוניציפליים, כולל ארגון הבריאות העולמי ומדינות רבות, הבחינו בדоказות וסגרו להימנעות מלהשתמש בתרופות אלו כחלק מהטיפול הרגיל בקורונה.

In recent days, photos of a 2003 article from Clarin, an Argentinian newspaper, have circulated widely on social media. Users sharing these images claim that the article is definitive proof that COVID-19 is "nothing new," suggesting that the disease we now know as COVID-19 existed long before the global outbreak in late 2019. This claim has sparked confusion and debate, raising questions about the origins of COVID-19 and the accuracy of historical reporting on coronaviruses.

To understand this claim, it is important to provide context about coronaviruses and the evolution of the COVID-19 pandemic. Coronaviruses are a large family of viruses known to cause illnesses ranging from the common cold to more severe diseases. Before 2019, notable coronavirus outbreaks included Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) in 2002-2003 and Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) in 2012. Both SARS and MERS were caused by different types of coronaviruses, which are related to, but distinct from, the virus responsible for COVID-19.

The article in question, published in Clarin in 2003, reportedly discusses the SARS outbreak, which was caused by the SARS-CoV coronavirus. Social media users have interpreted references to "coronavirus" in the article as evidence that COVID-19 existed at that time. However, this reflects a misunderstanding of both virology and medical terminology. In 2003, scientists already knew of several coronaviruses, some of which caused mild illnesses in humans. The SARS outbreak was caused by a novel coronavirus identified as SARS-CoV, which was new to science at the time but not related to COVID-19 except by its broader virus family.

COVID-19 is the name given to the disease caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019. While SARS-CoV-2 shares similarities with previous coronaviruses, it is genetically distinct and was not known to infect humans before the 2019 outbreak. The term "coronavirus" in earlier articles and scientific literature refers to the virus family, not specifically to SARS-CoV-2 or the COVID-19 disease. This is a critical distinction overlooked in the social media claim.

Fact-checking analysis reveals that the Clarin article from 2003 does not mention COVID-19 or SARS-CoV-2, as neither existed nor was identified at that time. Instead, the article is likely discussing the SARS outbreak and the general knowledge of coronaviruses at the time. The confusion arises from the use of the term "coronavirus," which is not synonymous with COVID-19. In scientific and medical contexts, "coronavirus" refers broadly to a virus family, while "COVID-19" specifically refers to the disease caused by SARS-CoV-2.

In conclusion, the claim that the 2003 Clarin article proves COVID-19 is "nothing new" is inaccurate. The article reflects contemporary understanding of coronaviruses and the SARS outbreak, not the existence of COVID-19. The current pandemic is caused by a novel virus first discovered in 2019, and equating earlier mentions of "coronavirus" with COVID-19 is misleading. This highlights the importance of careful interpretation of historical sources and scientific terminology, especially in the context of viral outbreaks.

최근 몇일간 아르헨티나 신문 클라린(Clárín)에서 2003년에 게재된 기사 사진이 소셜 미디어에서 폭넓게 유포되고 있다. 이 사진을 공유하는 사용자들은 이 기사가 현재 알려진 코로나19(COVID-19)가 "새로운 것이 아니다"는 것을 입증하는 확실한 증거라고 주장하며, 현재의 코로나19가 2019년 말의 글로벌 대유행 이전부터 존재했다고 말하고 있다. 이 주장은 코로나19의 출처에 대한 혼란과 논쟁을 일으켰으며, 코로나바이러스에 대한 역사적 보도의 정확성에 대한 의문을 제기하고 있다.

이 주장이 무엇을 의미하는지 이해하기 위해서는 코로나바이러스와 코로나19 팬데믹의 진화에 대한 맥락을 제공하는 것이 중요하다. 코로나바이러스는 감기부터 더 심각한 질병까지 다양한 질병을 일으키는 큰 바이러스 가족이다. 2019년 이전에 발생한 유명한 코로나바이러스 폭발 사례에는 2002-2003년에 발생한 중증 급성 호흡기 증후군(SARS)과 2012년에 발생한 중동 호흡기 증후군(MERS)이 있다. SARS와 MERS는 각각 다른 종류의 코로나바이러스에 의해 유발되었으며, 이 바이러스들은 코로나19의 원인인 바이러스와 관련이 있지만, 다른 종류이다.

논쟁의 중심이 되고 있는 2003년 클라린 기사는 SARS 폭발 사례를 다루고 있다고 보고 있다. 소셜 미디어 사용자들은 이 기사에서 언급된 "코로나바이러스"에 대한 언급을 코로나19가 이미 존재했음을 증거로 삼고 있다. 그러나 이는 바이러스학과 의학 용어에 대한 오해를 반영한다. 2003년 당시 과학자들은 이미 여러 종류의 코로나바이러스를 알고 있었으며, 그 중 일부는 인간에게 가벼운 질병을 일으켰다. SARS는 당시 과학적으로 알려지지 않은 새로운 코로나바이러스인 SARS-CoV에 의해 유발되었으며, 이 바이러스는 코로나19와 동일한 코로나바이러스 가족에 속하지만, 코로나19와는 관련이 없다.

코로나19는 중국 우한에서 2019년 말에 처음 발견된 새로운 코로나바이러스인 SARS-CoV-2에 의해 유발되는 질병으로 명명되었다. SARS-CoV-2는 이전 코로나바이러스와 유사한 특징을 가지고 있지만, 유전적으로 구분되며, 2019년 폭발 이전에는 인간에게 감염되지 않았다. 이전 기사 및 과학 문헌에서 사용된 "코로나바이러스"라는 용어는 코로나바이러스 가족을 지칭하는 것이며, SARS-CoV-2나 코로나19 질병을 특별히 지칭하는 것이 아니다. 이는 소셜 미디어에서 간과된 중요한 차이점이다.

사실 검증 분석에 따르면 2003년 클라린 기사는 코로나19나 SARS-CoV-2를 언급하지 않으며, 당시에는 이러한 바이러스나 질병이 존재하거나 확인되지 않았기 때문이다. 대신 이 기사는 SARS 폭발과 당시의 코로나바이러스에 대한 일반적인 지식을 다루고 있을 가능성이 높다. 혼란은 "코로나바이러스"라는 용어의 사용에서 비롯된다. 과학적 및 의학적 맥락에서 "코로나바이러스"는 바이러스 가족을 일반적으로 지칭하는 반면, "코로나19"는 SARS-CoV-2에 의해 유발되는 질병을 특별히 지칭한다.

결론적으로, 2003년 클라린 기사가 코로나19가 "새로운 것이 아니다"는 것을 증명한다는 주장은 부정확하다. 이 기사는 당시 코로나바이러스와 SARS 폭발에 대한 이해를 반영할 뿐, 코로나19의 존재를 증명하지 않는다. 현재의 팬데믹은 2019년에 처음 발견된 새로운 바이러스에 의해 유발되었으며, 이전의 "코로나바이러스" 언급을 코로나19와 동일시하는 것은 혼동을 일으킨다. 이는 특히 바이러스 폭발 상황에서 역사적 자료와 과학적 용어를 정확하게 해석하는 중요성을 강조한다.

article_content:
A viral social media post featuring a dramatic photograph claims that “thousands of birds fall dead amid the COVID-19 pandemic.” The image, widely shared across platforms, shows what appears to be a large number of bird carcasses strewn across a street or open field. The accompanying caption suggests a direct link between the COVID-19 pandemic and mass bird deaths, prompting alarm and concern among viewers.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is essential to examine both the context of the COVID-19 pandemic and the origins of the photograph. The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, is a disease that primarily affects humans. While there have been isolated reports of the virus infecting certain animals, including domestic pets and captive wildlife, there is no scientific evidence indicating that the virus has caused mass mortality events in wild bird populations.

Bird die-offs do occur periodically around the world, but they are typically linked to factors such as disease outbreaks specific to birds (like avian flu), extreme weather events, exposure to toxins, habitat disturbance, or collisions with man-made structures. During the early months of the COVID-19 pandemic, some news outlets did report unusual wildlife behaviors, often attributed to reduced human activity during lockdowns. However, claims of mass bird deaths directly resulting from the coronavirus are not supported by any credible scientific or governmental sources.

A closer examination of the photograph reveals that it has circulated online prior to the COVID-19 pandemic. In several instances, the image has been used in the past to illustrate unrelated bird mortality events, such as those caused by weather phenomena or localized poisoning. Reverse image searches show that the photograph can be traced back to reports from prior years, where it was associated with specific, documented events unrelated to COVID-19.

Moreover, ornithological and public health organizations have not reported any global or regional incidents of birds dying en masse due to the coronavirus. While certain avian species can be susceptible to strains of avian influenza or suffer from environmental hazards, the assertion that COVID-19 has caused thousands of birds to fall dead lacks scientific foundation.

The spread of such misinformation is not uncommon during global crises. The COVID-19 pandemic has been accompanied by a surge in rumors and false claims, often amplified by striking imagery or anecdotal accounts. These posts can generate unnecessary fear and distract from legitimate public health information.

In conclusion, the claim that thousands of birds have died as a direct result of the COVID-19 pandemic is not supported by scientific evidence. The photograph in question predates the pandemic and has been misrepresented to suggest a connection that does not exist. While bird die-offs do happen for various reasons, COVID-19 has not been identified as a cause. Social media users are urged to verify the origins and context of images and claims before sharing them further.

Virallik kazanan bir sosyal medya gönderisi, "Kovid-19 pandemisi sırasında binlerce kuş ölüyor" iddiasını içeren dramatik bir fotoğrafla sunuyor. Geniş şekilde paylaşılan bu resim, sokak ya da açık alanda yığılmış gibi görünen büyük sayıda kuş cesetlerini gösteriyor. Etkinlik açıklaması, Kovid-19 pandemisi ile kütle kuş ölümleri arasında doğrudan bir bağ olduğunu öne sürerek izleyicilerde korku ve endişe yaratıyor.

Bu iddianın geçerliliğini değerlendirmek için hem Kovid-19 pandemisinin hem de fotoğrafın kökenini incelemek gerekir. Kovid-19 pandemisi, yeni koronavirüs SARS-CoV-2 tarafından neden olan bir hastalıktır ve insanlara öncelikle etki eder. Kovid-19'un bazı hayvanlara, evcil hayvanlara ve avludaki doğa alanındaki hayvanlara bulaştığı izole raporlar vardır; ancak bu virüsün doğa kuş popülasyonlarında kütle ölümleri olaylarına neden olduğu bilimsel bir kanıt yoktur.

Kuş ölüm olayları dünyada periyodik olarak meydana gelir; ancak bu genellikle kuşlara özgü hastalıklar (örneğin kuş gribi), aşırı hava olayları, zehirli maddelere maruziyet, habitat bozulmaları veya insan yapımı yapılarla çarpışmalar gibi faktörlere bağlıdır. Kovid-19 pandemisinin başlangıç aylarında bazı haber kaynakları, kilise kapanışları sırasında insan aktivitesinin azalması nedeniyle sıra dışı doğa davranışları rapor etti. Ancak bu, Kovid-19'un doğrudan neden olduğu kütle kuş ölümleri iddiaları, güvenilir bilimsel veya kamu kurumları kaynaklarından desteklenmemektedir.

Fotoğrafın daha dikkatlice incelenmesi, bu resmin Kovid-19 pandemisi öncesi internette dolaştığını göstermektedir. Geçmişte bu resim, hava olayları veya yerel zehirlenmeler gibi ilişkisiz kuş ölüm olaylarını örneklemek için kullanılmıştır. Ters görüntü aramaları, bu fotoğrafın önceki yıllarda belirli ve belgeli olaylarla ilişkili olduğu, Kovid-19 ile ilgisi olmayan tarihlere kadar izlenebileceğini göstermektedir.

Ayrıca kuş bilimi ve halk sağlığı kurumları, Kovid-19'un neden olduğu kütle kuş ölümleri hakkında herhangi bir küresel veya bölgesel olay rapor etmemiştir. Belirli kuş türleri kuş gribi gibi virüs türlerine karşı hassas olabilir veya çevresel tehlikelerden etkilenir; ancak Kovid-19'un binlerce kuşun ölümesine neden olduğu iddiası bilimsel temele dayanmamaktadır.

Globel krizler sırasında bilgi yanlışlamalarının yayılması yaygın bir durumdur. Kovid-19 pandemisi, çarpıcı görseller ya da anekdotlara dayalı haberlerle birlikte, kanıtların eksik olduğu yanlış haberlerin artmasına neden olmuştur. Bu tür gönderiler, gerekli halk sağlığı bilgilerini dağıtmaktan uzaklaşarak gereksiz korkular yaratmaktadır.

Sonuç olarak, Kovid-19 pandemisinin doğrudan neden olduğu binlerce kuş ölüm iddiası bilimsel kanıtlarla desteklenmemektedir. Sorulan fotoğraf pandemi öncesi tarihlendirilmiştir ve bu bağlamda yanlış bir bağlantıya yol açmak için yanlış yorumlanmıştır. Kuş ölüm olayları çeşitli nedenlerle meydana gelir; ancak Kovid-19, bu olayların nedeni olarak belirlenmemiştir. Sosyal medya kullanıcıları, görüntüleri ve iddiaları paylaşmadan önce kaynaklarını ve bağlamını doğrulamaları önerilir.

The idea of intentionally exposing people to COVID-19 through so-called “contagion parties” has circulated on social media and in some communities since the early days of the pandemic. Advocates for this approach claim that by encouraging people—especially the young and healthy—to get infected, communities can reach herd immunity faster, thus ending the epidemic sooner. However, public health experts and epidemiologists caution that this strategy is not only flawed in theory but also dangerous in practice.

To understand the claim, it is important to revisit the concept of herd immunity. Herd immunity occurs when a large portion of a population becomes immune to an infectious disease, either through previous infection or vaccination, making the spread of the disease from person to person unlikely. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, before vaccines were available, some speculated that allowing the virus to run its course through less vulnerable groups might hasten the end of the crisis.

However, the reality of COVID-19 is far more complex. Unlike diseases such as chickenpox, where so-called “chickenpox parties” were historically arranged due to the relative predictability of the illness in children, COVID-19 is unpredictable and can cause severe illness or death in people of all ages, including those previously considered low-risk. The emergence of new variants, some more transmissible or severe, further complicates the idea of intentional exposure.

Furthermore, COVID-19’s potential for long-term effects, known as “long COVID,” means that even mild infections can have lasting and debilitating consequences. This risk is not confined to older adults or those with underlying medical conditions; young, otherwise healthy individuals have also reported ongoing symptoms long after their initial illness.

From a public health perspective, encouraging or organizing events where the virus is deliberately spread runs counter to the principles of disease control. Such gatherings can accelerate the spread of the virus, overwhelm healthcare systems, and lead to preventable hospitalizations and deaths. During surges, hospitals have faced shortages of beds, staff, and critical equipment, further endangering both COVID-19 patients and those in need of treatment for unrelated medical emergencies.

The development and widespread availability of effective vaccines has fundamentally changed the path to ending the COVID-19 epidemic. Vaccination provides a safe and controlled way to build immunity in the population, reducing transmission, severe illness, and death without the risks associated with natural infection.

In summary, the claim that COVID-19 contagion parties will make the epidemic end faster is not supported by scientific evidence or public health guidance. Intentionally exposing people to the virus carries significant risks, both to individuals and to society as a whole. The most effective and safest way to move toward the end of the COVID-19 epidemic remains widespread vaccination, continued surveillance, and adherence to proven public health measures—not deliberate outbreaks.

article_content:
A recent social media post has circulated a photograph purportedly showing officials washing raw chicken with chlorine and Ace, a popular household bleach brand. The post claims that this practice is putting the population at risk of poisoning, raising concerns about food safety and government oversight. This article examines the veracity of the claims and provides context on standard practices for food sanitation, the dangers of improper chemical use, and the risks to public health.

First, it is important to understand the context in which chemical washing is used in poultry processing. In some countries, including the United States and parts of Europe, poultry is routinely washed in dilute chlorine solutions to reduce bacterial contamination such as salmonella and campylobacter. These solutions are strictly regulated, and the concentrations used are considered safe for human consumption when the chicken is properly rinsed and cooked. However, the use of chlorine in poultry processing is controversial and banned in some regions, such as the European Union, due to concerns about chemical residues and the masking of poor hygiene standards.

The social media post, however, goes further by claiming that officials are also using Ace, a commercial bleach, to wash chicken. Household bleach typically contains sodium hypochlorite at much higher concentrations than those permitted for food processing. The use of household bleach in food preparation is not approved by any food safety authority due to the high risk of poisoning. Exposure to sodium hypochlorite at these concentrations can lead to severe health consequences, including irritation of the digestive tract, nausea, vomiting, and even damage to internal organs.

Upon analysis of the photograph, it appears that the chicken is being handled in an informal setting, possibly as part of a food safety demonstration or an industrial cleaning process. There is no clear evidence that the chicken is being prepared for sale or consumption after being washed with Ace. Further, official food safety standards strictly prohibit the use of household cleaning products on food intended for human consumption. Such practices, if they were occurring, would constitute a serious violation of health regulations and be subject to legal action.

Fact-checking the claim, there is no documented evidence from official sources that food safety officials or poultry processors use household bleach like Ace in the preparation of chicken for public consumption. The use of chlorine in regulated, dilute concentrations is sometimes permitted, but not household bleach. The widespread sharing of images and claims without context can lead to public misunderstanding and fear. It is also possible the image in question has been misrepresented, staged, or taken out of context.

In conclusion, while regulated use of chlorine in poultry processing is a legitimate, if controversial, practice, there is no credible evidence that officials are washing chicken with Ace bleach and exposing the population to poisoning. The claim, as stated in the social media post, is misleading and unsupported by current food safety guidelines or documented incidents. Consumers are urged to rely on verified information from food safety authorities and to critically evaluate sensational claims circulated on social media platforms.

اکثریت کے معاشرتی ایکسچنجرز نے ایک ایسی تصویر کی شیئر کی ہے جس میں اعلیٰ حکام کو چھوٹی سی کلورین کی سطح پر گھاس کے چکور کو غسل دینے کے دکھائی دے رہے ہیں، جس کے ساتھ ہی ایک معروف گھریلو چھوٹی سی کلورین بنیادی تیاری کے ساتھ چکور کو غسل دے رہے ہیں۔ اس پوسٹ کا دعویٰ ہے کہ یہ تہذیبی اور سلامتی کے اہم خطرات کی وجہ سے عام لوگوں کو سبزیوں کی نشست کے خطرات سے نکال دے رہا ہے، جو کہ غذا کی سلامتی اور حکومتی نگرانی کے تحفظ کے تجربات کو بڑھاوا دے رہا ہے۔ اس مقالے میں یہ دعویٰ کی حقیقت کا جائزہ لیا جائے گا اور غذا کی سلامتی کی معاہدہ شدہ ریٹنگ، غلط طریقہ کار کے کیمیکل استعمال کے خطرات اور عام لوگوں کی صحت کے خطرات کے بارے میں معلومات فراہم کی جائے گی۔

پہلے ہم اس بات کا جائزہ لینا ہو گا کہ کیمیکل غسل کیا ہے، جو کہ پکواو کے عمل میں استعمال ہوتا ہے۔ بعض ممالک میں، جیسے امریکہ اور یورپ کے کچھ حصوں میں، پکواو کے عمل میں کلورین کی ہلکی سطحیں استعمال کی جاتی ہیں، جو کہ سالمونلا اور کمپیلو بکتری جیسی بیکٹیریا کی تعداد کو کم کرنے کے لیے استعمال کی جاتی ہیں۔ یہ سطحیں ایک خاص طریقہ کار کے تحت نگرانی کی جاتی ہیں، اور جب چکور کو صحیح طریقہ سے ہلکا کیا جائے اور پکا کیا جائے تو انسانی غذا کے لیے ایک سیکیورٹی سطح کا حامل ہوتی ہیں۔ تاہم، کلورین کا استعمال پکواو کے عمل میں متنازعہ ہے، اور بعض علاقوں میں، جیسے یورپی یونین، اس کا استعمال ممنوع ہے، کیمیکل باقیات اور ناقص ہائیگین کی سطح کے خطرات کی وجہ سے۔

تاہم، اس معاشرتی ایکسچنجرز کا دعویٰ یہ ہے کہ حکام نے چکور کو ایسی چھوٹی سی کلورین بنیادی تیاری کے ساتھ غسل دیا ہے، جو کہ گھریلو چھوٹی سی کلورین کی تیاری ہے۔ گھریلو چھوٹی سی کلورین معمولی سطح سے زیادہ کلورین کی سطح کا حامل ہوتی ہے، جو کہ غذا کے تیاری کے لیے منظور نہیں ہے، کیونکہ اس کے استعمال کا خطرہ بہت زیادہ ہے۔ اس کلورین کی سطح پر اکثریت کے افراد کو بہت سی صحت کے خطرات کا سامنا کرنا پڑتا ہے، جیسے دہی کے ٹریکٹ کی تیزی، گلٹی، پیچھا، اور دماغی اعضاء کے نقصان کی وجہ سے۔

تصویر کے جائزہ کے بعد، یہ ظاہر ہوتا ہے کہ چکور کو ایک غیر رسمی ماحول میں ہاتھ سے پکواو کے عمل میں لے لیا جا رہا ہے، ممکنہ طور پر غذا کی سلامتی کی نمائش یا صنعتی صفائی کے عمل میں۔ چکور کو اس غسل کے بعد فروخت یا استعمال کے لیے تیار کرنے کے بارے میں کوئی واضح دلیل نہیں ہے۔ اور رسمی غذا کی سلامتی کے معاہدہ شدہ معیار میں، غذا کے لیے گھریلو صفائی کے اشیاء کا استعمال ممنوع ہے۔ ایسی تحریکیں، اگر واقع ہوئیں، صحت کے قوانین کی شدید خلاف ورزی ہوگی اور قانونی کارروائی کی جائے گی۔

دیکھے ہوئے دعویٰ کو جائزہ لیا جائے تو، کوئی رسمی ذرائع سے ثابت دلیل نہیں ہے کہ غذا کی سلامتی کے حکام یا چکور کے تیار کرنے والے افراد ایسی گھریلو چھوٹی سی کلورین بنیادی تیاری کے ساتھ چکور کو تیار کر رہے ہیں۔ معمولی سطح پر کلورین کا استعمال کبھی کبھی مجاز ہے، لیکن گھریلو چھوٹی سی کلورین نہیں۔ عام طور پر تصویر اور دعویٰ کی شیئر کیے جانے کے باوجود، عام لوگوں میں غلط فہمی اور خوف پیدا ہوسکتا ہے۔ یہ بھی ممکن ہے کہ تصویر گم ہو گئی ہو یا اس کا اصل مطلب نکال لیا گیا ہو۔

خاتمہ کے طور پر، معاہدہ شدہ کلورین کا استعمال پکواو کے عمل میں ایک درست، مگر متنازعہ ریٹنگ ہے، لیکن حکام کو چکور کو چھوٹی سی کلورین بنیادی تیاری کے ساتھ غسل دینے کا کوئی ثابت دلیل نہیں ہے جو کہ عام لوگوں کو سبزیوں کی نشست کے خطرات سے نکال دے رہا ہے۔ اس معاشرتی ایکسچنجرز کا دعویٰ، جیسا کہ اس مقالے میں دیا گیا ہے، غلط اور غیر محفوظ ہے۔ عام لوگوں کو غذا کی سلامتی کے حکام سے ثابت معلومات پر اعتماد کرنا چاہیے اور معاشرتی ایکسچنجرز پر دھوکا دہندہ دعویٰ کی جانچ کرنا چاہیے۔

article_content:
Social media platforms like Facebook continue to be hotbeds for health misinformation, particularly concerning COVID-19. A recent wave of posts and videos circulating online claim that drinking or inhaling seawater can prevent COVID-19 infection. These claims have garnered attention, with some users sharing personal anecdotes or unsubstantiated testimonials, prompting concern among health professionals about the potentially dangerous consequences.

To understand the origins of this claim, it's important to note that misinformation often thrives during public health crises, exploiting uncertainty and fear. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, various supposed remedies — from herbal concoctions to off-label medication use — have been promoted online. The assertion that seawater, whether consumed or inhaled, can prevent COVID-19 is the latest in a long line of pseudoscientific advice.

The core claim hinges on the idea that seawater, due to its salt content and perceived "purifying" properties, can either kill the virus or boost the immune system sufficiently to ward off infection. Some posts suggest that gargling, drinking, or even inhaling mist from seawater can cleanse the respiratory tract or neutralize the virus. However, a careful examination of scientific knowledge and medical guidelines exposes these assertions as baseless.

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, spreads primarily through respiratory droplets and contact with contaminated surfaces. Effective prevention strategies established by global health authorities include vaccination, wearing masks, practicing good hand hygiene, and maintaining social distancing. There is no scientific evidence that drinking or inhaling seawater has any effect on preventing or treating COVID-19. In fact, ingesting seawater can be harmful, leading to dehydration, electrolyte imbalances, and potential kidney damage. Seawater is not sterile; it contains a range of microorganisms and pollutants that pose health risks if consumed or inhaled.

Inhaling seawater mist, whether from natural sources or nebulized solutions, does not cleanse the lungs or respiratory tract of viruses. The respiratory system's mucous membranes are sensitive, and exposure to high concentrations of salt can irritate tissues, potentially exacerbating respiratory problems rather than alleviating them. Medical professionals strongly advise against introducing non-sterile substances into the nose, mouth, or lungs.

Moreover, the spread of misinformation suggesting seawater as a preventative measure is particularly concerning because it may lead individuals to neglect proven strategies such as vaccination and mask-wearing. False confidence in unproven remedies can increase the risk of contracting and spreading COVID-19, undermining broader public health efforts.

In summary, the claim that drinking or inhaling seawater prevents COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. Such practices can be harmful and distract from effective prevention measures. Health authorities urge the public to rely on verified information from reputable sources and to follow established guidelines for COVID-19 prevention and care. Social media users should exercise caution before sharing or acting on health advice found online, especially when it lacks scientific backing.

شبکه‌های اجتماعی مانند فیسبوک همچنان به عنوان مراکزی برای اطلاعات نادرست در زمینه سلامتی عمل می‌کنند، به ویژه در مورد کووید-19. موجی از پست‌ها و ویدئوها در اینترنت جریان دارد که ادعا می‌کنند مصرف یا تنفس آب دریا می‌تواند ابتلا به کووید-19 را جلوگیری کند. این ادعاهای مطرح شده توجه زیادی را جلب کرده‌اند، به طوری که برخی کاربران تجربیات شخصی یا ادعاهایی بدون پشتیبانی علمی به اشتراک گذاشته‌اند که باعث نگرانی متخصصان بهداشتی در مورد پیامدهای خطرناک احتمالی آن شده است.

برای درک مبدأ این ادعا، باید توجه داشت که اطلاعات نادرست معمولاً در مواقع بحران سلامت عمومی، با استفاده از عدم قطعیت و خوف، رشد می‌کند. از شروع بحران کووید-19، چندین راه‌حل مطرح شده است، از جمله عصاره‌های گیاهی تا استفاده از داروها در خارج از دستورالعمل، که از طریق اینترنت تبلیغ شده است. ادعای اینکه آب دریا، اگر مصرف یا تنفس شود، می‌تواند ابتلا به کووید-19 را جلوگیری کند، آخرین نمونه از مشاوره‌های غیر علمی است.

این ادعا بر اساس ایده اصلی است که به دلیل محتوی نمک و خواص "پاک کننده" اش، آب دریا می‌تواند ویروس را از بین ببرد یا سیستم ایمنی را به اندازه کافی تقویت کند تا ابتلا را جلوگیری کند. برخی پست‌ها ادعا می‌کنند که شستشو با آب دریا، مصرف آن یا هرگونه تنفس از بخار آن می‌تواند مسیرهای تنفسی را پاک کند یا ویروس را متعادل کند. با این حال، بررسی دقیق دانش علمی و دستورالعمل‌های پزشکی این ادعاهای را بدون پایه علمی نشان می‌دهد.

کووید-19 به دلیل ویروس SARS-CoV-2 ایجاد می‌شود و اصلی‌ترین روش انتقال آن از طریق قطرات تنفسی و تماس با سطوح آلوده است. راه‌های مؤثر جهت جلوگیری از ابتلا که توسط نهادهای بهداشت جهانی تعیین شده است شامل واکسن‌دهی، پوشیدن ماسک، بهداشت دست و نگهداشتن فاصله اجتماعی است. هیچ دلیل علمی وجود ندارد که مصرف یا تنفس آب دریا به جلوگیری یا درمان کووید-19 کمک کند. به علاوه، مصرف آب دریا می‌تواند خطرناک باشد و باعث ترکیب نامناسب الکترولیت، خشکی و آسیب به کلیه‌ها شود. آب دریا به طور کامل بهداشتی نیست و شامل میکروارگانیسم‌ها و آلاینده‌هایی است که اگر مصرف یا تنفس شوند، خطراتی برای سلامتی ایجاد می‌کنند.

تنفس از بخار آب دریا، اگر از منابع طبیعی یا محلول‌های نبوز باشد، مسیرهای تنفسی یا ریه‌ها را از ویروس پاک نمی‌کند. غشاها و بافت‌های مخاطی سیستم تنفسی حساس هستند و مواجهه با غلظت بالای نمک می‌تواند بافت‌ها را تحریک کرده و ممکن است مشکلات تنفسی را تشدید کند در حالی که آن را بهبود نمی‌دهد. پزشکان به طور قاطع به کاربران توصیه می‌کنند که مواد غیر بهداشتی را در گوش، دهان یا ریه‌ها وارد نکنند.

علاوه بر این، انتشار اطلاعات نادرست که آب دریا را به عنوان راه‌حل جلوگیری از ابتلا معرفی می‌کند، به خصوص اینکه ممکن است افراد اقدام به نادیده گرفتن روش‌های اثبات شده مانند واکسن‌دهی و پوشیدن ماسک کنند، بسیار نگران کننده است. اعتماد غلط به راه‌حل‌های بدون اثبات می‌تواند خطر ابتلا و پخش کووید-19 را افزایش دهد و باعث شود که تلاش‌های بزرگتر در زمینه بهداشت عمومی اثر نکند.

به طور خلاصه، ادعای مصرف یا تنفس آب دریا برای جلوگیری از کووید-19 توسط اطلاعات علمی پشتیبانی نمی‌شود. این روش‌ها ممکن است خطراتی ایجاد کنند و از روش‌های مؤثر جلوگیری از ابتلا فاصله بگیرند. نهادهای بهداشت از عموم مردم می‌خواهند به اطلاعاتی که از منابع معتبر حاصل شده است، وابسته باشند و دستورالعمل‌های اثبات شده را برای جلوگیری و درمان از کووید-19 اجرا کنند. کاربران شبکه‌های اجتماعی باید با حساسیت قبل از اشتراک گذاشتن یا اقدام بر اساس اطلاعات بهداشتی در اینترنت، به ویژه اگر آنها بدون پشتیبانی علمی باشند، دقت کنند.

The claim circulating on social media asserts that pathogenic viruses do not exist, citing German biologist Stefan Lanka, who allegedly proved this point in court. This statement has gained attention in certain online communities, prompting a need for a thorough examination of its accuracy and context.

Stefan Lanka is a German biologist known for his controversial views on virology, particularly his rejection of the scientific consensus regarding the existence and causality of viruses in diseases. Lanka’s notoriety largely stems from his public skepticism about HIV and, more notably, his challenge regarding the measles virus. He has argued that viruses such as measles are not pathogenic agents and even questioned their very existence.

The reference to a court case relates to a highly publicized legal proceeding in Germany. In 2011, Lanka offered a financial reward for scientific proof of the existence of the measles virus, which a medical doctor, David Bardens, sought to claim by submitting published studies. The case went to court after Lanka refused to pay, arguing that the submitted evidence did not meet his criteria. In 2015, the regional court in Ravensburg initially ruled in favor of Bardens, ordering Lanka to pay the reward. However, upon appeal in 2016, the Higher Regional Court of Stuttgart reversed the decision, not based on the non-existence of the measles virus, but rather on legal technicalities surrounding the prize conditions and the interpretation of what constituted “proof.”

It is crucial to clarify that the court did not rule on the scientific existence or non-existence of pathogenic viruses. Courts do not adjudicate scientific facts but instead interpret legal issues such as contract terms and the fulfillment of agreements. The reversal of the judgment did not constitute a scientific finding against the existence of viruses or their pathogenicity. Instead, it highlighted procedural and contractual ambiguities.

From a scientific standpoint, the existence of pathogenic viruses is overwhelmingly supported by a century of research in microbiology, virology, and epidemiology. Viruses such as measles, influenza, HIV, and SARS-CoV-2 have been isolated, studied, and linked conclusively to specific diseases through reproducible experiments, genetic sequencing, electron microscopy, and epidemiological data. The pathogenicity of viruses—their ability to cause disease—is fundamental to modern medicine and public health, evident in the success of vaccines and antiviral treatments.

The claim that Stefan Lanka “proved” the non-existence of pathogenic viruses in court misrepresents both the legal outcome and the scientific reality. The court did not address or validate Lanka’s scientific views; it only ruled on contractual matters. Moreover, Lanka’s position stands in stark contradiction to decades of validated scientific work. While scientific debate and skepticism are valuable, Lanka’s claims have not been substantiated by the broader scientific community.

In summary, the assertion that pathogenic viruses do not exist, as “proven” in court by Stefan Lanka, is incorrect. The court case did not settle any scientific debate but rather resolved a legal dispute over a prize offer. article_content:
A widely shared social media post claims that consuming a mixture of the juice of ten lemons, honey, ginger, onion, and ten garlic cloves three times a day is a recipe that both "prevents the coronavirus" and "helps recover from the virus." This assertion has been circulating in various forms since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, often accompanied by endorsements of natural remedies or traditional practices. In this article, we examine the validity of this claim and consider what is currently known about COVID-19 prevention and recovery.

**Context and Background**

Since the emergence of COVID-19, misinformation and unproven remedies have spread rapidly across social media platforms. Many of these remedies involve household items or natural substances such as garlic, ginger, honey, and lemon, which are commonly believed to boost immunity or fight infections. While these ingredients are often part of home remedies for colds and flu, COVID-19 is caused by a novel coronavirus (SARS-CoV-2), and its prevention and treatment require evidence-based approaches.

**Analysis of the Claim**

The claim suggests that a combination of lemon juice, honey, ginger, onion, and garlic, taken three times daily, can prevent infection with the coronavirus and aid in recovery for those already infected. Let's break down the components:

- **Lemon Juice** is high in vitamin C and often associated with immune support. However, there is no evidence that vitamin C alone can prevent or cure COVID-19.
- **Honey** has soothing properties and is sometimes used to relieve coughs, but it does not possess antiviral activity against SARS-CoV-2.
- **Ginger** and **Garlic** are touted for their anti-inflammatory and antimicrobial properties, but scientific studies do not demonstrate effectiveness against coronavirus infection in humans.
- **Onion** has some traditional uses for respiratory symptoms, but there is no scientific proof that it prevents or treats COVID-19.

While these ingredients may offer general health benefits and might help relieve mild symptoms such as sore throat or cough, none have been proven to prevent infection with SARS-CoV-2 or to speed recovery from COVID-19.

**Current Evidence and Recommendations**

Public health authorities recommend a combination of vaccination, hand hygiene, mask-wearing in certain situations, and physical distancing as the most effective ways to prevent COVID-19. For those infected, supportive care and, in some cases, antiviral medications or other medical interventions are the recommended treatments, especially for severe cases.

There is no credible scientific evidence to support the idea that any food, supplement, or home remedy can prevent coronavirus infection or serve as a cure. In fact, relying on unproven remedies may lead individuals to delay seeking proper medical care, potentially worsening outcomes.

**Conclusion**

The claim that consuming a mixture of lemon juice, honey, ginger, onion, and garlic three times daily can prevent or cure COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. While these ingredients are generally safe when used in moderation and may provide comfort for minor symptoms, they are not substitutes for proven preventive measures or medical treatment. It is important to rely on credible sources and evidence-based guidance when seeking to prevent or treat COVID-19.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated widely, claiming that the salaries of deputies in Guatemala have been suspended due to the COVID-19 crisis. This statement has generated significant discussion and confusion among the public, raising questions about its accuracy and the broader context surrounding government actions during the pandemic. In this article, we examine the veracity of this claim and provide an overview of the situation regarding the remuneration of Guatemalan deputies amid the COVID-19 crisis.

Guatemala, like many countries, faced enormous challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic. The health crisis prompted the government to implement measures aimed at controlling the spread of the virus, supporting the health care system, and providing economic relief to vulnerable populations. These measures included lockdowns, travel restrictions, and the allocation of emergency funds to various sectors. As the pandemic placed significant strain on the national budget, there was increased scrutiny of public spending, including the compensation received by elected officials.

The core claim in the social media post suggests that the salaries of deputies—members of Guatemala’s Congress—were suspended in response to the pandemic. This would imply a significant and unprecedented move, as the salaries of lawmakers are typically protected by law and considered essential for the functioning of legislative bodies. In Guatemala, deputies are elected to represent the interests of their constituents and are responsible for passing laws, overseeing government actions, and debating public policies. Their salaries are established by law and funded through the national budget.

Upon reviewing official statements, media reports, and legislative announcements from the period of the COVID-19 crisis, there is no evidence to support the claim that deputies’ salaries were suspended. While discussions about austerity measures and salary reductions for public officials did take place—reflecting public concern about government spending during a time of hardship—no official decree or law suspended the salaries of congressional deputies. In some instances, there were proposals to reduce or donate part of the salaries of high-ranking officials, including deputies, to support pandemic-related efforts, but these initiatives were voluntary and not universally adopted.

Furthermore, the legislative work continued throughout the pandemic, albeit with adjustments to procedures and greater reliance on remote or socially distanced sessions. Deputies continued to receive their salaries and benefits in accordance with the law. There were delays or modifications to certain payments in isolated cases, but these were related to administrative processes and not a blanket suspension of salaries.

In conclusion, the claim that the salaries of deputies in Guatemala were suspended due to the COVID-19 crisis is not supported by available evidence. While the pandemic did lead to increased debate over public spending and calls for solidarity among government officials, deputies continued to receive their salaries throughout the crisis. As always, it is important for the public to seek reliable sources and verify information before sharing it, especially in times of uncertainty.

У последnjih данима, пост је широм социјалних мрежа ширен, који тврди да су плата дејтима у Гватемалу паузирана због кризе коронавируса. Ово тврђење је изазвало значајну дискусију и забринутост у јавности, подигајући питања о његовој тачности и широком контексту акција владе током пандемије. У овом чланку анализирамо тачност овог тврђења и дајемо увод о ситуацији у којој су дејти у Гватемалу добивали плата током кризе коронавируса.

Гватемала, као и многе других земаља, је током пандемије коронавируса извела велике изазове. Здравствена криза је узроковала да влада примени умерене мере које су имале за циљ да контролишу ширење вируса, подрже здравствен систем и да пруже економски утешења најосетљивијим популацијама. Ове мере су укључивале забране излаза, ограничења путовања и распоред узимања екстралокалних фондова у различите секторе. Када је пандемија значајно подешавала национални буџет, јавно је било већа критика према јавним трошковима, укључујући и плата изабраних представника.

Кључно тврђење у социјалној мрежи тврди да су плата дејтима – члановима Гватемалског КОНГРЕСА – паузирана у одговору на пандемију. Ово би значило значајну и неочекивану мере, јер плата законодатеља увек је заштитена законом и сматрана је есенцијалном за функционисање законодавних тела. У Гватемалу, дејти су изабрани да представљају интересе својих грађана и одговорни су за пренос закона, надзор над радом владе и дискусију јавних политика. Их плата је установљена законом и финансирана из националног буџета.

После прегледа официјалних изјава, медијских извештаја и законодавних објава током пандемије коронавируса, нема доказа који би подржавали тврђење да су плата дејтима паузирана. Иако су дискусије о мерах аустеритета и смањењу плата за јавне службенике узимале место – што је одражавало јавну забринутост о трошковима владе у време тежина – није постојала официјална одлука или закон који је паузирана плата законодатеља. У неким случајевима су били предлоги да се смањи или да се донира део плата високих службеника, укључујући дејти, за подршку пандемијским напорима, али су ови иницијативе били добровољни и нису били усвојени у целости.

Додатно, законодавски рад је настављен током пандемије, али је имао промене у процедурама и већу зависност од удаљеног или социјално одвојеног састанка. Дејти су настављали да добијају плата и користе одговарајуће одлуке. Били су одложене или промене у неким плаћањима у изолованим случајевима, али су ово били повезано са административним процесима, а не са укупном паузираном плата.

In recent years, ivermectin has become the subject of heated debate and widespread misinformation regarding its potential role in treating and preventing COVID-19. The claim that "ivermectin is a drug that cures and prevents COVID-19" has circulated widely across social media platforms, fueling confusion among the public. A careful examination of scientific evidence and guidance from health authorities is essential to assess the accuracy of this claim.

Ivermectin is an anti-parasitic medication approved for use in humans to treat conditions like river blindness and certain intestinal worms. It has also been used in veterinary medicine for decades. Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, laboratory studies suggested that ivermectin might inhibit the replication of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, in cell cultures. This led to interest in its potential as a treatment or preventive measure against the disease.

However, laboratory findings do not always translate into clinical effectiveness. The concentrations of ivermectin used in these studies were much higher than those safely achievable in humans. As a result, researchers initiated clinical trials to evaluate whether ivermectin could benefit people infected with COVID-19 or help prevent infection.

Over the past few years, multiple studies and clinical trials have been conducted worldwide. The results have been mixed, with some early, small-scale studies suggesting possible benefits, while larger, more rigorous trials found no significant effect of ivermectin in reducing COVID-19-related illness, hospitalization, or death. These larger studies are considered more reliable due to their design and sample size.

Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization and national health agencies, have reviewed the available evidence and do not recommend the use of ivermectin for either the treatment or prevention of COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. They emphasize that the current data are insufficient to support its routine use for COVID-19 and caution that misuse of ivermectin can lead to harmful side effects, especially when taken in doses intended for animals or outside medical supervision.

Furthermore, the belief that ivermectin "cures and prevents" COVID-19 can be dangerous, as it may discourage people from seeking proven and effective interventions, such as vaccination, wearing masks, and following public health guidelines. Vaccines remain the most effective tool in preventing severe illness and death from COVID-19.

In conclusion, the claim that ivermectin cures and prevents COVID-19 is not supported by robust scientific evidence. While research into potential COVID-19 treatments continues, ivermectin has not been proven safe or effective for this purpose. People should rely on validated treatments and preventive measures and consult healthcare professionals for guidance regarding COVID-19 management.

અત્યારના વર્ષોમાં, ઇવર્મેક્ટિન કોવિડ-19 ની સારવાર અને રોગપ્રતિરોધ માટે તેના સંભાવિત ભૂમિકા વિશે ઉનાં વાતાવરણ અને વિસ્તૃત અસંચારનો વિષય બની ગયો છે. "ઇવર્મેક્ટિન એ એક દવા છે જે કોવિડ-19 ને સારવાર અને રોગપ્રતિરોધ કરે છે" તે કલ્પના સામાજિક મીડિયા પ્રસારણ પર વિસ્તૃત રીતે ફરી ફરી પ્રસારિત થઈ છે, જે જનતાને એટલી બધી ભ્રમાંથી ભરી દીધી છે. આ કલ્પનાની સાચી સમાનતાની મૂલ્યાંકન માટે વૈજ્ઞાનિક પુરાવા અને આરોગ્ય સંસ્થાઓની માર્ગદર્શન નો સાવચેતીપૂર્વક અવલોકન જરૂરી છે.

ઇવર્મેક્ટિન એ એન્ટી-પેરાસિટિક દવા છે જે માનવ શરીરમાં નદીની અંધારી અને કેટલાક આંતરડાના પ્રાણીઓની સારવાર માટે મંજૂરી આપવામાં આવી છે. તે પણ વેટરીનરી ચિકિત્સામાં દાખલ થયેલ છે. કોવિડ-19 મહામારીની શરૂઆતમાં લેબોરેટરી અભ્યાસોની પ્રારંભિક નિરીક્ષણ પ્રમાણે ઇવર્મેક્ટિન સારવાર માટે કોવિડ-19 ના કારણભૂત વાયરસ સારવાર માટે સાંકેતિક કોશિકાઓમાં SARS-CoV-2 નું પ્રાપ્તિ બંધ કરી શકે છે, જે તેની કોવિડ-19 ની સારવાર અથવા રોગપ્રતિરોધ માટેની સાંભળવા માટેની માંગ ઉત્પન્ન કરી છે.

તેમાંથી એક વિચાર છે કે લેબોરેટરી પરિણામો ક્લિનિકલ પ્રભાવની સાથે સમાન રીતે નથી સ્થળાંતર કરતાં. આ અભ્યાસોમાં ઇવર્મેક્ટિનની સાંખ્યાઓ માનવ માટે સુરક્ષિત રીતે પ્રાપ્ત કરી શકાય તેની સાંખ્યાઓ કરતાં વધુ હતી. તેથી, અભ્યાસકરોએ કોવિડ-19 ના રોગીઓને કે રોગપ્રતિરોધ માટે ઇવર્મેક્ટિનની કેટલી મદદ થઈ શકે છે તેની મૂલ્યાંકન માટે ક્લિનિકલ ટ્રાયલ્સ શરૂ કરી દીધી હતી.

પૂર્વાનુમાન અને અંતર્ગત વિવિધ અભ્યાસો અને ક્લિનિકલ ટ્રાયલ્સ સાથે અંતર્ગત વિવિધ દેશોમાં અનેક અભ્યાસો અને ક્લિનિકલ ટ્રાયલ્સ કરવામાં આવ્યા છે. પરિણામો વિવિધ હતા, કેટલાક પ્રારંભિક છોટા અભ્યાસો માટે સંભવિત લાભો પ્રસ્તુત કર્યા હતા, જ્યારે મોટા, વધુ મજબૂત ટ્રાયલ્સ કોવિડ-19 સંબંધિત રોગ, હોસ્પિટલિઝેશન અથવા મૃત્યુ માટે ઇવર્મેક્ટિનના કોઈ મહત્વપૂર્ણ પ્રભાવ નથી મળ્યો. આ મોટા અભ્યાસો તેમના ડિઝાઇન અને નમૂનાની આંકેલ કારણે વધુ માન્યતાપૂર્વક માનવામાં આવ્યા છે.

વર્લ્ડ હેલ્થ ઓર્ગેનાઇઝેશન અને દેશના આરોગ્ય એજન્સીઓ સહિત મુખ્ય આરોગ્ય સંસ્થાઓએ ઉપલબ્ધ પુરાવાની મૂલ્યાંકન કરી છે અને કોવિડ-19 ની સારવાર અથવા રોગપ્રતિરોધ માટે ક્લિનિકલ ટ્રાયલ્સ બાહેર ઇવર્મેક્ટિનનો ઉપયોગ મંજૂર કરવામાં આવ્યો નથી. તેમણે સ્પષ્ટ કર્યું છે કે વર્તમાન પુરાવા કોવિડ-19 માટે ઇવર્મેક્ટિનનો સામાન્ય ઉપયોગ માટે યોગ્ય નથી અને તેની અસાધુપણાની વાપર નુકસાનકારક પરિણામો લાવી શકે છે, ખાસ કરીને જ્યારે પ્રાણીઓ માટે અસાધુપણાની સાંખ્યાઓ અથવા ચિકિત્સા સૂચના બાહેર લેવામાં આવે છે.

સાથે સાથે, ઇવર્મેક્ટિન "કોવિડ-19 ને સારવાર અને રોગપ્રતિરોધ કરે છે" તે વિશ્વાસ ખતરનાક હોઈ શકે છે, કારણ કે તે લોકોને પ્રમાણિત અને અસરકારક પ્રવૃત્તિઓ, જેમ કે ટીકાકરણ, માસ્ક ધરાવવું અને સામાજિક આરોગ્ય માર્ગદર્શનો અનુસરવું ન હોય તેવી ભ્રમાંથી બચાવી શકે છે. ટીકાકરણ કોવિડ-19 માટે ગંભીર રોગ અને મૃત્યુ પર સૌથી અસરકારક ઉપાય છે.

સમાપ્તિ તરીકે, ઇવર્મેક્ટિન કોવિડ-19 ને સારવાર અને રોગપ્રતિરોધ કરે છે તે સુસ્થિર વૈજ્ઞાનિક પુરાવા દ્વારા સમર્થિત નથી. જ્યારે કોવિડ-19 ની સારવાર માટેના અન્વેષણ ચાલુ રહે છે, તેની સાથે ઇવર્મેક્ટિન માટે સુરક્ષિત અને અસરકારક પુરાવા હજુ સુધી પ્રાપ્ત થયેલ નથી. લોકો પ્રમાણિત સારવાર અને રોગપ્રતિરોધ ઉપાયો પર આધાર રાખે અને કોવિડ-19 ની સારવાર માટે ચિકિત્સાશાસ્ત્રીઓની સલાહ લેવી જરૂરી છે.

A video circulating on social media has sparked alarm and outrage, with claims that the Mexican Air Force is throwing bodies of people infected with COVID-19 onto the beaches of Acapulco. The footage, widely shared across various platforms, appears to show a military aircraft flying low over a coastal area, while objects are released from the plane and land on the beach. The accompanying posts allege these are corpses of COVID-19 victims, disposed of in this shocking manner as part of government efforts to control the pandemic’s spread.

To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to examine several key aspects: the context of the video, the history of military activity in the region, and official protocols for handling COVID-19 fatalities in Mexico.

First, Acapulco is a major tourist destination in the state of Guerrero, Mexico, known for its beaches and resorts. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the city experienced significant disruptions, including travel restrictions, temporary closures, and increased public health measures. However, there have been no credible reports from Mexican authorities or international organizations supporting the idea that the military has engaged in such extreme actions as dumping bodies on public beaches.

Analysis of the video itself reveals inconsistencies with the claim. Military aircraft are used for a range of purposes, including training exercises, supply drops, and aerial surveillance. In many cases, videos of planes releasing objects are misinterpreted; they may be dropping cargo, emergency supplies, or even conducting practice missions involving non-lethal materials. The footage does not show clear evidence of human bodies nor any indication that the items dropped are related to COVID-19 casualties. Furthermore, the logistics and practicality of disposing bodies in such a public and unsanitary manner run counter to standard health and safety protocols enacted during the pandemic.

Official Mexican government policy requires that bodies of those deceased from COVID-19 be handled with strict sanitary procedures. These include the use of protective equipment by medical personnel, prompt burial or cremation, and clear documentation. There has been significant public scrutiny of pandemic management in Mexico, but no verified incidents of body dumping, particularly by military forces, have been reported in Acapulco or elsewhere.

Social media posts spreading this claim often lack corroborating evidence and rely on sensationalism. Misinformation around the pandemic has been pervasive, driven by fear, confusion, and the rapid circulation of unverified content. Experts warn that such unfounded rumors can cause unnecessary panic, stigmatization, and hinder public health efforts.

In conclusion, there is no substantiated proof that the Mexican Air Force has thrown bodies of COVID-19 victims onto Acapulco's beaches. The video in question is more likely to depict routine military or civil operations unrelated to the pandemic. The claim appears to be a fabrication, amplified through social media without basis in fact. It is essential for the public to approach such alarming reports with skepticism and seek information from reliable sources before accepting or spreading them.

सामाजिक सञ्जालमा प्रसारित एउटा भिडियोले आशंका र आक्रोश उत्पन्न गरेको छ, जसमा मेक्सिको वायु सेना एक्सपेल्सिओ रोग भएका व्यक्तिहरुको शवहरु एकपटक एकपटक अकापुल्को तटमा फेकिरहेको देखिन्छ। यो भिडियो, विभिन्न प्लेटफार्ममा व्यापकरूपमा साझा गरिएको छ, जसमा एउटा सैन्य विमान एक तटीय क्षेत्रमा कम उडान गर्दै छ र विमानमा वस्तुहरु छोडिएको छ र तटमा बर्बाद गरिएको छ। साथमा लेखिएका पोस्टहरु यी वस्तुहरु एक्सपेल्सिओ रोग भएका व्यक्तिहरुको शवहरु हुन सक्छन्, जसले प्रायः सरकारको प्रयासले एक्सपेल्सिओ फैलावट नियन्त्रण गर्न अप्रत्यक्ष रूपमा शव तटमा फेकिरहेको छ।

अफवाह अस्वीकृत गर्न यो विषयमा केहि महत्वपूर्ण बिषयहरु अध्ययन गर्न आवश्यक छः भिडियोको संदर्भ, क्षेत्रमा सैन्य गतिविधिको इतिहास, र मेक्सिकोमा एक्सपेल्सिओ विपत्ति मृतकहरुको संचालनको आधिकारिक प्रोटोकोलहरु।

पहिलो, अकापुल्को गुएरेरो राज्यको एक महत्वपूर्ण पर्यटन स्थल छ, जसको तट र रिसोर्टहरु प्रसिद्ध छन्। कोभिड-१९ महामारीको कालमा शहरले धेरै अस्थिरता अनुभव गरेको छ, जसमा यातायात सीमा, चर्तु बन्द र सार्वजनिक स्वास्थ्य उपायहरु शामिल छन्। तथापि, मेक्सिको सरकार वा अंतरराष्ट्रिय संगठनहरु द्वारा यो विषयमा कुनै विश्वसनीय रिपोर्ट छैन जसमा भनिएको छ कि सैन्य शक्ति एक अत्याधुनिक विधि जसमा शव तटमा फेकिरहेको छ।

भिडियोको विश्लेषण अफवाह अस्वीकृत गर्न महत्वपूर्ण असंगतिहरु देखिन्छ। सैन्य विमान विभिन्न कार्यहरुका लागि प्रयोग गरिन्छ, जसमा अभ्यास, सामग्री ड्रोप र एरियल सर्भिस समावेश छ। धेरै अवसरमा विमान वस्तुहरु छोडिएको भिडियोहरु गलत अनुवाद गरिन्छ, जसमा यही सामग्री ड्रोप वा आपातकालीन सामग्री वा अप्रत्यक्ष अस्पृश्य सामग्रीको अभ्यास गर्ने मिशन छ। भिडियोमा मानव शरीरहरुको स्पष्ट देखावट छैन र कोभिड-१९ मृतकहरुको वस्तुहरुको संकेत छैन। यसले प्रायः सार्वजनिक र अपरिच्छद ढंगले शव फेकिरहेको विधिको लागि लॉजिस्टिक्स र व्यावहारिकता असंगत छ, जसले महामारीको कालमा आचार्य र सुरक्षा नियमहरु छोडिदिन छ।

मेक्सिको सरकारको आधिकारिक नीति एक्सपेल्सिओ विपत्ति मृतकहरुको शवहरुको सानो नियमहरु छ। यसमा चिकित्सा कर्मचारीहरुको रक्षा सामग्रीको उपयोग, त्वरित दफनाव वा अग्निकारण र स्पष्ट दस्तावेजीकरण समावेश छ। महामारीको प्रबंधनको सार्वजनिक निगरानी धेरै छ, तर अकापुल्को वा अन्यत्र शव फेकिरहेको कुनै पुष्टि गरिएको घटना छैन।

सामाजिक सञ्जालमा यो अफवाह फैलाउने पोस्टहरु अधिक तथ्य देखाउँदैन र अत्यधिक समाचार वा अत्यधिक विपणन अवलम्बन गर्छ। कोभिड-१९ बारे अफवाह धेरै छ, जो भय, भ्रम र अनुसंधान गर्न अनुमति दिने अनुमान बाट विस्तार भएको छ। विशेषज्ञहरु चेतावनी दिन्छन् कि अधारहीन अफवाह अप्रत्यक्ष भय, चिह्न र जनस्वास्थ्य प्रयासहरुको अवरोध गर्न सक्छ।

तदनुसार, मेक्सिको वायु सेना एक्सपेल्सिओ मृतकहरुको शवहरु अकापुल्को तटमा फेकिरहेको वास्तविक आधार छैन। भिडियोमा विषय अधिक तंत्रिक सैन्य वा सामाजिक कार्य छ, जो महामारी संग असंबंधित छ। अफवाह अधिक रूपमा सामाजिक सञ्जाल द्वारा बढाइएको छ र तथ्यांक अधिक छैन। सार्वजनिकले यी चिंताजनक रिपोर्टहरु अस्वीकृत गर्न आवश्यक छ र संदेह गर्नु आवश्यक छ र विश्वसनीय स्रोतहरु बाट जानकारी लिएर त्यसलाई ग्रहण गर्न वा फैलाउनु आवश्यक छ।

A recent social media post claims that the President of Mexico has proposed a tax of 500 pesos for each pet, with the intention of funding social programs related to COVID-19. The claim has generated considerable debate and concern among pet owners and animal welfare advocates. This fact-checking article examines the validity of this claim by analyzing official statements, recent legislative activity, and the broader context of Mexico’s response to COVID-19.

First, it is important to understand the role of the President of Mexico, currently Andrés Manuel López Obrador, in proposing new taxes. In Mexico, tax proposals are typically drafted as part of the federal budget by the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit, then submitted to Congress for debate and approval. While the president can suggest or support new fiscal measures, any such proposal must follow this legislative process and is subject to public scrutiny and debate.

The claim specifically states that a 500-peso tax per pet has been proposed to support social programs addressing the impact of COVID-19. Since the start of the pandemic in early 2020, Mexico has implemented a variety of social programs, including cash transfers, health support, and employment initiatives, aimed at mitigating the economic and health effects of COVID-19. Funding for these programs has generally come from existing tax revenues, budget reallocations, and international loans. There has been significant public discussion about increasing taxes or introducing new ones, but most have focused on areas such as income, corporate profits, or digital services.

To date, there is no record of an official proposal from the president or the Mexican government to introduce a tax specifically targeting pet ownership for COVID-19 related social programs. A review of recent press conferences, official statements, and legislative documents reveals no mention of such a tax. Animal-related policies in Mexico have historically focused on welfare, vaccination, and control of stray populations, not on imposing taxes on pet owners.

The idea of a "pet tax" is not entirely unheard of in other countries; some cities and municipalities worldwide have experimented with licensing fees or taxes to support animal welfare initiatives. However, these are usually modest and have local, not national, scope. A tax as high as 500 pesos per pet, applied nationwide, would represent a significant new burden, and its implementation would likely require extensive legislative debate and public notice.

Furthermore, the claim ties the supposed tax directly to COVID-19 social programs. The Mexican government’s strategy has not included pet-related taxes as a funding source. Instead, the emphasis has been on maintaining economic stability, supporting vulnerable populations, and strengthening the healthcare system through more traditional means.

In conclusion, after a thorough review of available information, there is no evidence to support the claim that the President of Mexico has proposed a 500-peso tax per pet to fund COVID-19 social programs. The claim does not align with current government policy, official records, or recent legislative activity. It appears to be unfounded and should be viewed as misinformation unless further substantiated by credible sources or official announcements.

Recently, a claim has circulated on social media suggesting that an herb referred to as "holy leaf" or "momo" can cure COVID-19 and aid patients experiencing breathing difficulties. This assertion has garnered attention among communities seeking natural remedies for the virus, which continues to affect populations globally. Given the seriousness of COVID-19 and the importance of reliable health information, it is crucial to examine the validity of this claim.

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, is a respiratory illness that can range from mild symptoms to severe complications, including difficulty breathing and organ failure. Since its emergence, scientists and healthcare professionals have worked tirelessly to identify effective treatments and preventive measures. Currently, approved therapies for COVID-19 include antiviral drugs, supportive care, and vaccines developed through rigorous clinical trials. While alternative and traditional medicines have been explored for their potential benefits, their efficacy and safety are subject to scientific scrutiny.

The herb mentioned in the claim, known as "holy leaf" or "momo," is not widely recognized in mainstream medical literature or among commonly documented medicinal plants. In some regions, "holy leaf" may refer to plants such as Ocimum sanctum (commonly known as holy basil or tulsi) or Plectranthus amboinicus (known as Indian borage or Cuban oregano). The term "momo" could also denote various local herbs depending on cultural context. These plants have traditional uses in herbal medicine, often valued for their purported anti-inflammatory, antimicrobial, or respiratory benefits.

Despite traditional uses, there is currently no scientific evidence to support the claim that "holy leaf" or "momo" can cure COVID-19. No herbal remedy, including those referenced as "holy leaf" or "momo," has been demonstrated through clinical trials to eliminate the SARS-CoV-2 virus or serve as a stand-alone cure for the disease. Healthcare authorities emphasize that while some herbs may help alleviate minor symptoms such as cough or sore throat, they cannot substitute approved medical treatments or emergency care, especially for severe cases of COVID-19.

The assertion that "holy leaf" or "momo" helps patients breathe warrants careful consideration. Respiratory support for COVID-19 patients is typically managed through oxygen therapy, medications to reduce inflammation, and, in critical cases, mechanical ventilation. While some herbal remedies may provide subjective relief for mild respiratory discomfort, they are not substitutes for medical interventions required in cases of respiratory distress related to COVID-19.

In summary, while traditional herbs like those described as "holy leaf" or "momo" may have a place in complementary medicine, there is no credible scientific evidence to support the claim that they cure COVID-19 or offer substantial aid to patients struggling to breathe due to the virus. Relying solely on these herbs for treatment risks delaying necessary medical care and could lead to serious health consequences. Individuals experiencing symptoms of COVID-19 or respiratory difficulty should seek guidance from qualified healthcare professionals and adhere to recommended treatments and preventive measures.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that the coronavirus, or COVID-19, is not a virus but rather an “expanded exosome” generated by exposure to 5G wireless technology. This assertion combines several scientific-sounding ideas and conspiracy theories, but lacks support from credible evidence. Here, we break down the claim and examine the facts.

First, let’s address the central elements: exosomes, coronavirus, and 5G.

Exosomes are small vesicles, or bubble-like structures, that are produced by cells in the body. These microscopic particles are released by cells to carry proteins, lipids, and genetic material to other cells. Exosomes play important roles in cell communication and immune responses. They are not pathogens themselves, and they do not cause infectious diseases.

Coronavirus refers to a family of viruses, including the novel coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which causes the disease COVID-19. Coronaviruses are so named because of their crown-like appearance under a microscope. The existence of coronaviruses has been documented for decades, and SARS-CoV-2 was identified and genetically sequenced by scientists in early 2020. The symptoms and transmission of COVID-19 have been extensively studied by the global scientific community.

The claim that coronavirus is actually an “expanded exosome” caused by 5G appears to conflate these distinct scientific concepts. Some proponents of this theory point to superficial similarities between exosomes and viruses—they are both microscopic, membrane-bound particles found in the body. However, structural and functional differences are well-established. Viruses like SARS-CoV-2 have distinct genetic sequences, proteins, and mechanisms for infecting host cells that exosomes do not possess.

Additionally, there is no scientific evidence that 5G wireless technology, which refers to the fifth generation of mobile networks, can create exosomes or viruses in the human body. 5G operates using radiofrequency electromagnetic fields, which are non-ionizing and incapable of altering cellular structure or causing biological particles like exosomes to “expand” or morph into viruses. The claim that 5G can cause or spread COVID-19 has been repeatedly debunked by health organizations and independent experts.

The confusion may stem from early research that described similarities in size between exosomes and some viruses, but a close examination of their genetic material and function shows clear differences. Laboratory techniques can distinguish between viral particles and exosomes. Furthermore, the spread of COVID-19 has closely followed patterns of human-to-human transmission, not the rollout of 5G networks.

In summary, the social media claim that coronavirus is an “expanded exosome” caused by 5G is not supported by scientific evidence. Coronaviruses are distinct, well-characterized viruses, and exosomes are naturally occurring cellular vesicles with different purposes. 5G technology does not cause biological particles to transform or expand. The overwhelming consensus in the scientific and medical communities is that COVID-19 is caused by a virus, not by wireless technology or exosomes.

Koronavirus er distinkte, veldefinerede virus, og eksosomer er naturligt forekommende cellevesikler med forskellige funktioner. 5G-teknologi forårsager ikke, at biologiske partikler transformerer eller udvider sig. Den overvældende konsensus i videnskabelige og medicinske fagmiljøer er, at COVID-19 forårsages af et virus, ikke af mobiltelefon-teknologi eller eksosomer.

A social media post recently claimed that “Chlorine Dioxide (CLO2) cures the bug that worries the governments all around the world so much.” The post, though brief, appears to suggest that chlorine dioxide is an effective remedy or cure for a widespread infectious disease – most likely referencing COVID-19, which has been a major global health concern in recent years.

To examine this claim, it is important to understand what chlorine dioxide is, its common uses, and the scientific evidence regarding its safety and efficacy in treating human illnesses.

Chlorine dioxide is a chemical compound with disinfectant properties. It is widely used in industrial settings for water treatment, bleaching in the paper industry, and disinfecting medical equipment. Its utility stems from its ability to kill bacteria, viruses, and fungi on surfaces and in water. However, chlorine dioxide is not approved for ingestion or inhalation as a medical treatment for any disease in humans. Regulatory agencies such as the FDA and equivalent bodies in other countries classify chlorine dioxide as a hazardous substance when used outside its intended industrial applications, and warn against its use as a medicine.

The suggestion that chlorine dioxide “cures” a viral infection conflates its legitimate role as a disinfectant with its safety and efficacy within the human body. Chlorine dioxide is a strong oxidizing agent; when ingested or inhaled, it can cause serious side effects, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, dehydration, and even life-threatening complications. It does not have any recognized mechanism to target or eliminate viruses in living tissues without causing harm to the host.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, misinformation about chlorine dioxide circulated widely on social media, with some groups promoting it as a “miracle cure” under names such as “Miracle Mineral Solution” (MMS). Medical authorities around the world have repeatedly stated that there is no evidence supporting the use of chlorine dioxide in the prevention or treatment of COVID-19 or other viral illnesses. In fact, the promotion of chlorine dioxide as a cure has led to reports of poisoning and adverse health outcomes.

The core claim in the social media post—that chlorine dioxide cures the bug worrying governments worldwide—is not supported by credible scientific or medical evidence. While chlorine dioxide can kill pathogens on surfaces, it is not a safe or effective treatment for viral infections in humans. Amid ongoing concerns about misinformation surrounding COVID-19 treatments, a recent social media post claims that Fisiol, Mucosolvan, and Fluimucil are recommended for treating COVID-19. This article examines the validity of these claims, provides medical context, and analyzes their appropriateness as treatments for COVID-19.

Fisiol, Mucosolvan, and Fluimucil are all medications commonly used to address respiratory symptoms. Fisiol is a brand name for saline solutions, often used for nasal irrigation or inhalation to help clear mucus. Mucosolvan contains ambroxol, a mucolytic agent that helps thin and loosen mucus in the airways, making it easier to cough up. Fluimucil contains acetylcysteine, another mucolytic that reduces the thickness of mucus, facilitating its removal from the respiratory tract. These drugs are typically prescribed for conditions such as bronchitis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and other respiratory illnesses characterized by excessive or thick mucus.

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, can present with a wide range of symptoms, including fever, cough, shortness of breath, fatigue, and sometimes excessive mucus production, especially in severe cases. While managing respiratory symptoms is an important aspect of supportive care for COVID-19 patients, it is critical to differentiate between symptom relief and actual treatment of the disease.

International health authorities, including the World Health Organization and national medical bodies, have provided guidelines for COVID-19 treatment. These guidelines emphasize supportive care, including oxygen therapy, fluids, and medications to control fever and pain. For severe cases, antiviral agents, corticosteroids, and anticoagulants may be used under medical supervision. There is no evidence that mucolytic agents like ambroxol (Mucosolvan) or acetylcysteine (Fluimucil), or saline solutions (Fisiol), are directly recommended or endorsed as treatments for COVID-19 itself.

The use of Fisiol, Mucosolvan, and Fluimucil may provide symptomatic relief for patients experiencing congestion or thick mucus. However, these medications do not address the underlying viral infection or prevent complications such as pneumonia or acute respiratory distress syndrome, which can occur in COVID-19. It is important to note that indiscriminate use of mucolytics in viral infections may not always be beneficial and could potentially cause side effects, especially in patients with certain underlying conditions.

Moreover, recommending these medications as a standard COVID-19 treatment is misleading. While healthcare providers may prescribe them to manage specific symptoms in select patients, they are not a substitute for evidence-based COVID-19 therapies. Patients considering any medication should consult a healthcare professional for guidance tailored to their individual health status.

In conclusion, the claim that Fisiol, Mucosolvan, and Fluimucil are recommended for COVID-19 treatment is not supported by current medical guidelines. These drugs may offer relief for respiratory symptoms but are not recognized as primary treatments for COVID-19. Accurate information and guidance from qualified healthcare professionals are essential to ensure proper care and avoid the risks associated with inappropriate medication use.
