A claim circulating on social media alleges that a World Bank document proves COVID-19 was planned as early as 2017. The post suggests that the existence of such a document is evidence of foreknowledge or intentional planning of the pandemic, fueling conspiracy theories about the origins and handling of COVID-19. A close examination of the claim, the referenced World Bank documents, and the context surrounding them reveals that this assertion is misleading and not supported by the facts.

The claim centers on World Bank project documentation that references "COVID-19" and project timelines that appear to predate the outbreak, such as 2017. These documents are often cited in viral posts and videos as supposed proof that the pandemic was orchestrated or anticipated years before the first known cases of COVID-19 in late 2019.

To assess this claim, it is crucial to understand what these World Bank documents are and how the organization operates. The World Bank routinely develops and updates projects related to public health, disaster preparedness, and pandemic response. Many of these projects have long timelines, sometimes spanning decades, and are updated to address emerging crises as they arise.

In the case cited by social media posts, the documents in question are typically related to ongoing health sector projects that were initiated years before the COVID-19 pandemic. For instance, a project may have started in 2017 to address general pandemic preparedness, health infrastructure, or infectious disease control. When the COVID-19 pandemic emerged in 2019-2020, these projects were often amended or repurposed to address the specific challenges posed by the coronavirus. As a result, the project documentation was updated to include references to "COVID-19," even though the project’s initial approval date might be years earlier.

This standard practice of updating project documentation can create the appearance that COVID-19 was mentioned prior to its known existence. However, this is a misunderstanding of how project records are maintained and updated. The presence of "COVID-19" in a document with an earlier initial date does not indicate that the disease was known or planned in advance; rather, it reflects the adaptation of ongoing health projects to respond to the pandemic.

Additionally, there is no credible evidence from the World Bank or any reputable scientific source to support the idea that COVID-19 was intentionally planned or known prior to its emergence in Wuhan, China, in late 2019. The overwhelming consensus in the scientific and public health communities is that COVID-19 is caused by a novel coronavirus that crossed into humans in late 2019, leading to the global pandemic declared in 2020.

In summary, the claim that a World Bank document proves COVID-19 was planned since 2017 is based on a misinterpretation of routine project documentation practices. The references to COVID-19 in documents with earlier start dates reflect updates to existing projects, not evidence of prior knowledge or planning of the pandemic. Such claims contribute to misinformation and detract from efforts to address the ongoing impacts of the pandemic.

O afirmație care circulă pe rețelele sociale susține că un document al Băncii Mondiale dovedește că pandemia de COVID-19 a fost planificată încă din anul 2017. Postul sugerează că existența acestui document este dovadă de cunoștință anticipată sau planificare intenționată a pandemiei, alimentând teorii conspirative privind originea și gestionarea pandemiei de COVID-19. O examinare atentă a afirmației, a documentelor referite de Băncă Mondială și a contextului în care acestea se găsesc arată că această susținere este înșelătoare și nu este susținută de fapte.

Afirmația se bazează pe documentația referitoare la proiecte ale Băncii Mondiale care menționează „COVID-19” și pe termene de proiect care păreau să precede izbucnirea pandemiei, cum ar fi 2017. Aceste documente sunt adesea citate în postări virale și videoclipuri ca dovadă că pandemia a fost orchestrată sau anticipată ani înainte de primele cazuri cunoscute de COVID-19, în ultima parte a anului 2019.

Pentru a evalua această afirmație, este esențial să înțelegem ce sunt aceste documente ale Băncii Mondiale și cum funcționează organizația. Băncile Mondiale dezvoltă și actualizează în mod regulat proiecte legate de sănătate publică, pregătirea pentru dezastre și răspunsul la pandemii. Mulți dintre aceste proiecte au termene lungi, uneori decenii, și sunt actualizați pentru a aborda crizele emergente în măsura în care apar.

În cazul citat de postările de pe rețelele sociale, documentele în cauză sunt de obicei legate de proiecte în desfășurare din sectorul sănătății care au fost inițiate ani înainte de pandemia de COVID-19. De exemplu, un proiect poate fi pornit în 2017 pentru a aborda pregătirea generală pentru pandemii, infrastructura sănătății sau controlul bolilor infecțioase. Când pandemia de COVID-19 a izbucnit în 2019-2020, aceste proiecte au fost adesea modificate sau reutilizate pentru a face față provocărilor specifice legate de coronavirus. Astfel, documentația de proiect a fost actualizată pentru a include referințe la „COVID-19”, chiar dacă data de aprobare inițială a proiectului ar putea fi mai devreme.

Această practică standard de actualizare a documentației de proiect poate crea iluzia că „COVID-19” a fost menționat înainte de a fi cunoscut. Totuși, aceasta este o neînțelegere a modului în care sunt menținute și actualizate înregistrările de proiect. Prezența „COVID-19” într-un document cu o dată inițială mai veche nu indică faptul că boala a fost cunoscută sau planificată înainte; mai degrabă, reflectă adaptarea proiectelor existente pentru a răspunde pandemiei.

În plus, nu există dovezi credibile din partea Băncii Mondiale sau din partea oricărei surse științifice de încredere care să susțină ideea că pandemia de COVID-19 a fost planificată sau cunoscută înainte de apariția sa în China, în ultima parte a anului 2019. Consensul general în comunitatea științifică și a sănătății publice este că COVID-19 este cauzat de un coronavirus nou care a trecut în mod natural în om în ultima parte a anului 2019, ducând la pandemia globală declarată în 2020.

În concluzie, afirmația că un document al Băncii Mondiale dovedește că pandemia de COVID-19 a fost planificată din 2017 se bazează pe o neînțelegere a practicilor obișnuite de documentare a proiectelor. Referințele la „COVID-19” din documente cu date de început mai vechi reflectă actualizările proiectelor existente pentru a răspunde pandemiei, nu dovadă de cunoștință sau planificare anterioară a pandemiei. Asemenea afirmații contribuie la informația incorectă și scad eforturile de a face față impactului continuu al pandemiei.

A recent social media post claims that the Sputnik V vaccine is based on a “DNA adenovirus” that will be “part of your genetics.” This statement has generated confusion and concern about the vaccine's safety and mechanism of action. To clarify these issues, it is important to examine how the Sputnik V vaccine works, what a DNA adenovirus is, and whether the vaccine can alter a person’s genetic material.

Sputnik V, also known as Gam-COVID-Vac, is a COVID-19 vaccine developed by the Gamaleya Research Institute in Russia. It is based on a viral vector platform, meaning it uses a harmless virus (in this case, an adenovirus) to deliver genetic instructions to human cells. The purpose of these instructions is to prompt the body’s immune system to recognize and defend against the SARS-CoV-2 virus, which causes COVID-19.

Adenoviruses are common viruses that typically cause mild illnesses, such as the common cold. For vaccine purposes, the adenoviruses are modified so that they cannot replicate or cause disease in humans. In the Sputnik V vaccine, two different types of adenoviruses (Ad26 and Ad5) are used in two separate doses, enhancing the immune response.

The “DNA” aspect refers to the fact that adenoviruses are DNA viruses, meaning their genetic material is in the form of DNA rather than RNA. In the context of the vaccine, the adenovirus is engineered to carry the gene that codes for the spike protein of SARS-CoV-2. When the vaccine is administered, the adenovirus enters some human cells and delivers this gene. The cells then use it to temporarily produce the spike protein, which is recognized by the immune system, leading to the development of immunity.

The critical claim of the social media post is that the vaccine’s DNA will become “part of your genetics.” This is inaccurate. While the vaccine does introduce DNA into some of your cells, it does not integrate this DNA into your own genome. The adenoviral DNA remains separate from your chromosomes, and the cell machinery uses it only to make the spike protein for a short period. Eventually, the DNA and the spike protein are broken down and removed by the body. There is no credible scientific evidence or mechanism by which the DNA from the vaccine could become a permanent part of your genetic material.

Additionally, viral vector vaccines like Sputnik V have been used in other medical applications, including vaccines for Ebola and gene therapy, with no evidence that they alter recipients’ genomes.

In summary, while Sputnik V does use a DNA adenovirus as a delivery vehicle, the claim that it becomes “part of your genetics” is false. The vaccine does not alter your DNA or integrate foreign genetic material into your genome. Its design is to safely trigger an immune response, not to modify genetic makeup. Misinformation about vaccine technology can fuel unnecessary fear and vaccine hesitancy, making clear and accurate understanding essential during global public health efforts.

article_content:
A recent social media post has sparked confusion and concern, claiming that applesauce tested positive for COVID-19 and could transmit the disease. This claim has quickly gained traction online, leaving many consumers questioning the safety of their food and the possibility of transmission through packaged products. A closer examination of the facts reveals that the claim is misleading and not supported by scientific evidence.

To understand the issue, it is important to look at how COVID-19, the disease caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, is detected and transmitted. COVID-19 primarily spreads through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. Surfaces and objects can become contaminated with the virus, but the primary mode of transmission is person-to-person contact. While it is possible, though rare, to contract the virus by touching a contaminated surface and then touching the face, health authorities have consistently stated that the risk of contracting COVID-19 from food or food packaging is extremely low.

The claim that applesauce "tested positive" for COVID-19 likely stems from misunderstandings of how viral testing works. PCR (polymerase chain reaction) tests used to detect SARS-CoV-2 are designed to identify genetic material from the virus. In rare laboratory settings, these tests may sometimes detect genetic fragments of the virus in unexpected places, such as surfaces or non-living samples, due to contamination or improper handling. However, the presence of viral genetic material does not mean the virus is alive, infectious, or capable of causing disease. Detecting viral RNA on a food product like applesauce does not indicate that the applesauce can transmit COVID-19.

Furthermore, there is no credible evidence to suggest that commercially produced applesauce or any other packaged food product has been a source of COVID-19 infection. Food manufacturers follow strict hygiene and safety protocols to prevent contamination. If viral particles were present on a food package or inside a sealed product, they would not survive long enough to remain infectious, especially given the time required for packaging, shipping, and storage. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and other health organizations have repeatedly affirmed that foodborne transmission of COVID-19 is not a significant concern.

In summary, the claim that applesauce tested positive for COVID-19 and could transmit the disease is not supported by current scientific understanding or evidence. While traces of viral RNA can potentially be found on surfaces or objects under specific circumstances, this does not equate to a risk of infection. Consumers can continue to enjoy applesauce and other packaged foods without fear of contracting COVID-19 from them. Good hygiene practices, such as handwashing before eating, remain the most effective way to reduce the risk of illness.

Een recente sociale media post heeft verwarring en zorgen veroorzaakt, met de bewering dat appelsaus positief getest is op COVID-19 en het virus kan verspreiden. Deze bewering heeft snel online grip gekregen, waardoor veel consumenten de veiligheid van hun voedsel en de mogelijkheid van verspreiding via verpakte producten in twijfel trokken. Een nauwkeurige onderzoek van de feiten toont aan dat de bewering misleidend is en niet gesteund wordt door wetenschappelijk bewijs.

Om het probleem te begrijpen, is het belangrijk om te kijken hoe COVID-19, het ziekteverloop veroorzaakt door het SARS-CoV-2 virus, wordt gedetecteerd en verspreid. COVID-19 verspreidt zich vooral via ademhalingsdruppels wanneer een besmette persoon hoest, niezt of spreekt. Oppervlakken en objecten kunnen besmet worden met het virus, maar de primaire manier van verspreiding is persoon op persoon. Hoewel het mogelijk is, maar zeldzaam, om het virus te verkrijgen door een besmettelijk oppervlak aan te raken en daarna het gezicht te aantasten, hebben gezondheidsinstanties steeds benadrukt dat het risico op het verkrijgen van COVID-19 via voedsel of voedingsverpakkingen zeer laag is.

De bewering dat appelsaus "positief getest" is op COVID-19 komt waarschijnlijk uit verwarring over hoe virale tests werken. PCR (polymerase kettingreactie) tests die gebruikt worden om SARS-CoV-2 te detecteren zijn bedoeld om genetisch materiaal van het virus te identificeren. In zeldzame laboratoriumomstandigheden kunnen deze tests soms genetische fragmenten van het virus op onverwachte plekken, zoals oppervlakken of niet levende monsters, detecteren vanwege verontreiniging of onjuiste behandeling. Echter, de aanwezigheid van viraal genmateriaal betekent niet dat het virus levend, besmettelijk of ziekteverwekkend is. Het detecteren van viraal RNA op een voedselproduct zoals appelsaus wijst niet op het feit dat appelsaus het virus kan verspreiden.

Bovendien is er geen betrouwbare bewijsvoering die suggereert dat commercieel geproduceerde appelsaus of enige andere verpakte voedingsproducten een bron van besmetting met COVID-19 zijn. Voedingsfabrikanten volgen strenge hygiëne- en veiligheidsprotocollen om besmetting te voorkomen. Als virusdeeltjes aanwezig zouden zijn op een voedingsverpakking of binnen een gesloten product, zouden ze niet lang genoeg overleven om besmettelijk te blijven, vooral gezien de tijd die nodig is voor verpakking, verzending en opslag. De Centers for Disease Control and Prevention en andere gezondheidsinstanties hebben herhaaldelijk bevestigd dat voedselgerelateerde verspreiding van COVID-19 geen belangrijke zorg oplevert.

In samenvatting is de bewering dat appelsaus positief getest is op COVID-19 en het virus kan verspreiden niet gesteund door huidige wetenschappelijke kennis of bewijs. Hoewel sporen van viraal RNA onder bepaalde omstandigheden op oppervlakken of objecten kunnen worden gevonden, betekent dit niet dat er een risico op besmetting bestaat. Consumenten kunnen appelsaus en andere verpakte voedingsproducten zonder zorgen genieten. Goede hygiënepraktijken, zoals het wassen van de handen voor het eten, blijven de meest effectieve manier om het risico op ziekte te verlagen.

A recent social media post has circulated widely, claiming that the Wuhan laboratory is owned by Glaxo and is related to Pfizer, which distributes the vaccines for COVID-19. This statement suggests a direct ownership and operational link between the Wuhan Institute of Virology, GlaxoSmithKline (often referred to as Glaxo), and Pfizer—two major pharmaceutical companies involved in the development and distribution of COVID-19 vaccines. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to examine the ownership of the Wuhan lab, the relationships among the named companies, and their roles during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The Wuhan Institute of Virology (WIV) is a prominent research institution located in Wuhan, China. Established in 1956, WIV operates under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, a governmental organization in China. The institute is known for its research on virology, including work on coronaviruses. There is no credible evidence that GlaxoSmithKline owns, operates, or directly controls the Wuhan Institute of Virology. The institute is publicly funded and managed by Chinese governmental agencies.

GlaxoSmithKline (GSK) is a British multinational pharmaceutical company. While GSK has a significant presence in China and has entered into joint ventures and partnerships within the Chinese pharmaceutical market, none of these partnerships involve the ownership or management of the Wuhan Institute of Virology. The confusion may arise from GSK’s general business interests in China or from misinterpretations of public information about their activities in the country.

Pfizer is a separate, American multinational pharmaceutical corporation. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Pfizer, in partnership with the German biotech company BioNTech, developed and distributed one of the first mRNA vaccines for COVID-19. GSK was not involved in the development or distribution of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine. Instead, GSK collaborated with other companies, such as Sanofi, to develop their own vaccines. There is no documented corporate relationship between GSK and Pfizer related to COVID-19 vaccine distribution. Although large pharmaceutical companies sometimes have cross-licensing agreements or collaborate on certain projects, there is no evidence of any direct business relationship between GSK and Pfizer concerning the Wuhan Institute of Virology or the COVID-19 vaccines.

The claim also implies a conspiracy by suggesting that the same entities responsible for the creation of the virus are those profiting from the development and sale of vaccines. This narrative has been widely debunked by independent experts. The origin of COVID-19 is still under study, with the majority of scientific evidence pointing to a natural origin of the virus, though investigations continue.

In summary, the claim that the Wuhan laboratory is owned by Glaxo and is related to Pfizer, which distributes the vaccines for COVID-19, is not supported by factual evidence. The Wuhan Institute of Virology is not owned by GlaxoSmithKline or any other foreign pharmaceutical company, and there are no operational ties between the institute, GSK, and Pfizer regarding COVID-19 vaccine development or distribution.

A social media post claims, “Why is there a vaccine against COVID, but not for cancer, AIDS, or the common flu? This proves that there is no SARS-CoV-2 virus, which causes COVID.” This statement raises questions about the existence of vaccines for various diseases and draws a conclusion about the existence of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19. We examine the accuracy of these claims and provide context on vaccine development.

First, it is important to understand how vaccines work and why they are available for some diseases but not others. Vaccines are designed to train the immune system to recognize and fight specific pathogens, such as viruses or bacteria. The development of vaccines depends on a deep understanding of the disease-causing agent, its behavior in the body, and the immune response it provokes.

For COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, scientists were able to rapidly develop vaccines due to prior research on coronaviruses, technological advances in vaccine design, and the urgency of the pandemic. Multiple COVID-19 vaccines, using different technologies, have been authorized and widely distributed globally.

The claim that there is no vaccine for cancer, AIDS, or the common flu is misleading or inaccurate. Cancer is not a singular disease but a term for hundreds of different conditions characterized by uncontrolled cell growth. Some cancers are caused by viruses, such as cervical cancer by human papillomavirus (HPV) and liver cancer by hepatitis B virus (HBV). Vaccines exist against HPV and HBV, which help prevent these virus-induced cancers. However, most cancers are not caused by infectious agents, making vaccine development impossible or impractical for those types.

For AIDS, caused by the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), vaccine development has faced significant scientific challenges. HIV mutates rapidly and evades the immune system, making it difficult to create a vaccine that provides lasting protection. Researchers have been working on HIV vaccines for decades, and while some candidates are in trials, none have proven effective enough for widespread use yet.

The post also mentions the “common flu.” In reality, annual vaccines are available for influenza, commonly known as the flu. These vaccines are updated each year to match circulating strains, as the influenza virus mutates frequently. While the flu vaccine may not provide complete protection due to these mutations, it does reduce the risk of infection and severe illness.

The assertion that the presence of a COVID-19 vaccine “proves that there is no SARS-CoV-2 virus” is unfounded. The existence of a vaccine does not negate the existence of the virus; rather, it is evidence of the virus’s reality. SARS-CoV-2 has been isolated, sequenced, and studied extensively by scientists worldwide. COVID-19 vaccines are a direct response to the threat posed by the virus.

In summary, vaccines exist for some cancers, influenza, and COVID-19, but not yet for HIV/AIDS due to scientific hurdles. The development and availability of vaccines depend on the nature of the disease and the pathogen involved. The claim that the COVID-19 vaccine’s existence disproves the existence of SARS-CoV-2 is incorrect and not supported by scientific evidence.

Sotsiaalmeedias levitatakse väitel, et "Miks on vaktsiin kõrva jaoks, kuid mitte ka kancerile, AIDSile või tavalise külma kõrva? See näitab, et SARS-CoV-2 viiruse, mis põhjustab kõrva, ei ole olemas." See väide toob esile küsimusi vaktsiinide olemasolu erinevate haiguste suhtes ning järeldab SARS-CoV-2 viiruse olemasolu, mis põhjustab kõrva. Me analüüsime seda väite tõesust ja pakkume taustatundmatust vaktsiinide arendamise kohta.

Esimesena on oluline mõista, kuidas vaktsiinid toimivad ja miks need on olemas mõne haiguse jaoks, kuid mitte teistele. Vaktsiinid on mõeldud immuunsüsteemi hariduseks, et tunnistada ja vastata erinevate patogeenide, nagu viirused või bakterid, vastu. Vaktsiinide arendus sõltub tugevast teaduslikust mõistest haiguse põhjustavast agentist, selle käitumisest kehas ja immuunvastusest, mida see provotseerib.

Kõrva põhjustavaks on SARS-CoV-2 viirus, kuid teadlased suutisid kiiresti arendada vaktsiine põhjusel, et eelnevate koronaviiruse teadustööde tulemusena, vaktsiinide disaini tehnoloogilised edusammud ja kõrva pandeemia tõhusus. Mitmeid kõrva vaktsiine, mis kasutavad erinevaid tehnoloogiaid, on rahvusvahelistel kinnitatud ja laialdaselt jagatud.

Väide, et kancerile, AIDSile või tavalise külma kõrva ei ole vaktsiine, on väärne või ebatäpne. Kancer pole üksik haigus, vaid sõnastus sõltub sümboolsetest haigustest, millel on ülekontrollitud rakkude kasv. Mõned kancerid on põhjustatud viirustest, näiteks sõmbrakkerkanceri inimpapiloomiviruse (HPV) ja maksakanceri hepatiit B viiruse (HBV) tõttu. Vaktsiine on olemas HPV ja HBV vastu, mis aitavad ennetada neid viiruspõhjustatud kancerit. Kuid enamik kancerit ei põhjusta infektsioonivahendeid, mis teeb vaktsiinide arendamist nende tüüpide jaoks ebatavaliseks või ebaefektiivseks.

AIDS, mis on põhjustatud inimimmuunidefiitsiooniviruse (HIV) poolt, on teaduslikult suurt haigust, mille pärast on tehtud palju katseid. HIV muutub kiiresti ja vältib immuunsüsteemi, mis teeb keeruliseks vaktsiini loomise, mis pakkub kestlikku kaitset. Teadlased on töötanud HIV vaktsiini pärast aastakümneid, ja kui mõned kandidaadid on katsetusel, siis ei ole ühtegi tänaseni piisavalt tõhusat vaktsiini, mis oleks laialdaselt kasutusel.

Posti teisel osal mainitakse "tavalist külma kõrva". Tegelikult on igal aastal saadaval influenza vaktsiin, mis on tavaliselt tuntud kui külma kõrva. Need vaktsiinid uuendatakse igal aastal, et vastata kehale levivate strainidele, kuna influenza viirus muutub sageli. Kui külma kõrva vaktsiin ei pakkuda täielikku kaitset selle tõttu, siis see vähendab kõrva levikut ja tõhusust.

Väide, et kõrva vaktsiini olemasolu "tõendab, et SARS-CoV-2 viirust ei ole", on väärne. Vaktsiini olemasolu ei vähenda viiruse olemasolu, vaid see on näide selle olemasolust. SARS-CoV-2 on isoleeritud, sequeeritud ja uuritud maailma teadlaste poolt. Kõrva vaktsiinid on suunatud viiruse teatud ohtude vastu.

Kokkuvõttes on vaktsiine olemas mõne kanceri, influenza ja kõrva jaoks, kuid HIV/AIDS jaoks ei ole neid veel teaduslikult keeruliste hambadeta. A claim circulating on social media asserts that a study published in the scientific journal Nature shows that asymptomatic people do not transmit COVID-19. This assertion has generated considerable interest, as it challenges one of the key principles informing public health policies during the COVID-19 pandemic. To evaluate the accuracy of this statement, it is important to examine both the scientific literature and broader context regarding asymptomatic transmission.

Background and Context

Since the emergence of COVID-19, understanding how the virus spreads has been central to controlling the pandemic. Early in the outbreak, reports indicated that people infected with SARS-CoV-2 could transmit the virus before showing symptoms or even without ever developing symptoms (asymptomatic transmission). This insight significantly influenced mitigation measures such as mask mandates, physical distancing, and isolation guidelines.

The Claim and the Nature Study

The social media post claims that a study published in Nature demonstrates that asymptomatic individuals do not transmit COVID-19. This statement references a real scientific debate, as researchers have investigated the degree to which asymptomatic individuals contribute to the spread of the virus.

Some studies, including those published in reputable journals like Nature, have examined outbreaks or conducted contact tracing to assess transmission rates from asymptomatic individuals. In certain settings, particularly where rigorous contact tracing and isolation were implemented, these studies found low or even negligible secondary attack rates from documented asymptomatic cases. For instance, one study analyzed data from a mass testing campaign and concluded that there was no evidence of transmission from asymptomatic individuals in that specific context.

Fact-Checking Analysis

However, the claim that "asymptomatic people do not transmit COVID" overstates the scientific consensus and misrepresents the findings of individual studies. The majority of research indicates that asymptomatic and presymptomatic transmission is possible, even if it occurs at a lower rate than symptomatic transmission. Many studies, using different methodologies and conducted in diverse settings, have found that people without symptoms can and do spread SARS-CoV-2, sometimes unknowingly.

The Nature article cited in various posts typically refers to a study conducted in a highly controlled environment, possibly with extensive public health interventions such as isolation, quarantine, and universal masking. These specific circumstances may have reduced the likelihood of detecting asymptomatic transmission, but they do not provide definitive evidence that asymptomatic people never transmit COVID-19.

It is also important to distinguish between asymptomatic and presymptomatic individuals. The latter are those who have been infected and are contagious before symptoms develop. Multiple studies have confirmed that presymptomatic transmission plays a significant role in the spread of COVID-19.

Conclusion

The social media post is misleading. While some studies published in Nature and other journals have found low rates of transmission from asymptomatic individuals in particular settings, the overall body of scientific evidence supports the conclusion that asymptomatic people can, in fact, transmit COVID-19, albeit potentially at lower rates than those with symptoms. Public health recommendations continue to reflect this risk, emphasizing the importance of precautions regardless of symptom status.

A claim has circulated widely on social media stating that a nurse in the United States died after applying the COVID-19 vaccine. As vaccination efforts expanded across the country, stories of alleged adverse reactions to the vaccines have appeared online, often sparking public concern and hesitancy. This article examines the validity of the claim, provides relevant context, and analyzes available evidence.

Since the initial rollout of COVID-19 vaccines in late 2020, millions of healthcare workers, including nurses, were among the first groups to receive the vaccine. Given the high public interest and scrutiny of vaccine safety, any reported incident involving a healthcare worker and the vaccine quickly gained attention. The claim that a nurse died after receiving the COVID-19 vaccine has been repeated in various forms, sometimes referencing specific locations or individuals, but often lacking verifiable details.

Upon review, there are no confirmed reports from reputable sources, such as the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), or major news organizations, of a nurse in the United States dying as a direct result of receiving the COVID-19 vaccine. While there have been isolated reports of deaths among vaccine recipients, these cases have been thoroughly investigated by health authorities. The vast majority of reported deaths following vaccination have been found to be unrelated to the vaccine itself, with causes attributed to underlying health conditions or coincidental timing.

It is important to note that the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) collects reports of any health problems following vaccination, regardless of the likelihood of a causal relationship. These reports are not evidence of causation and are intended as a tool for monitoring potential safety signals. Health authorities review these reports and conduct investigations as necessary. To date, the COVID-19 vaccines authorized in the United States have been shown to be safe and effective for the vast majority of recipients, with serious adverse events being extremely rare.

The spread of unverified stories, such as the claim of a nurse dying after vaccination, can contribute to vaccine hesitancy and public fear. In cases where healthcare workers have experienced adverse events, transparency and thorough investigation are critical. When deaths have occurred in proximity to vaccination, health agencies have communicated findings openly and have not identified a pattern of deaths causally linked to the vaccine among nurses or other groups.

In conclusion, the claim that a nurse in the United States died after applying the COVID-19 vaccine is not supported by credible evidence. While any medical intervention carries potential risks, the available data indicate that COVID-19 vaccines are safe, and incidents of fatal outcomes directly caused by the vaccine are exceedingly rare. It is always important to consult reliable sources and health authorities when assessing vaccine safety claims.

A recent social media post has circulated widely, claiming that the Secretary of Health in Mexico has published a list of people who cannot be vaccinated. This assertion has sparked confusion and concern among many citizens, especially as Mexico continues its efforts to immunize the population against various diseases, including COVID-19. To clarify the matter, it is important to examine the facts, the practices of the Mexican health authorities, and the procedures typically followed for vaccination campaigns.

First, the Secretary of Health in Mexico, known as Secretaría de Salud, is the federal government agency responsible for public health policy, including vaccination programs. During the COVID-19 pandemic and in other large-scale immunization efforts, the agency has communicated guidance on vaccine eligibility and safety. These guidelines are generally based on scientific evidence and recommendations provided by national and international health organizations.

The claim that the Secretary of Health has published a formal “list” of individuals who cannot be vaccinated suggests the existence of an official document naming specific people or groups. However, a review of official communications, press releases, and the agency’s website indicates that no such published list exists. Instead, the Secretary of Health has periodically issued general recommendations outlining medical conditions or situations in which vaccination might be contraindicated or delayed. These recommendations are standard practice in many countries and are meant to ensure the safety and efficacy of vaccines.

Common examples of individuals advised to delay or avoid certain vaccines include people with severe allergic reactions to vaccine components, those experiencing active illness with fever, or individuals with specific immune system disorders. For the COVID-19 vaccine, for instance, the Secretary of Health has advised that people who have had a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) to a previous dose or to an ingredient in the vaccine should not receive that vaccine. Pregnant or breastfeeding women, children under a certain age, and people with certain health conditions have also been given tailored guidance, depending on the most current scientific data.

It is important to distinguish between these general medical recommendations and the idea of an explicit “list” of prohibited individuals. The Secretary of Health has not published a document naming individuals or even detailed lists of groups who categorically cannot be vaccinated. Instead, health professionals evaluate each person’s medical history and current health status to determine vaccine eligibility. This approach aligns with international health protocols designed to maximize safety while promoting widespread immunization.

In summary, the social media post claiming that the Secretary of Health in Mexico published a list of people who cannot be vaccinated is misleading. While the agency provides general guidelines on who should avoid vaccination under specific circumstances, it has not released a formal, comprehensive list naming individuals or groups. The decision to vaccinate is based on individual medical assessment and the latest scientific recommendations, rather than on a static, published list.

A social media post circulating recently claims that to prevent COVID-19, individuals should take azithromycin and ivermectin during the first three days of experiencing symptoms. This recommendation raises concerns among medical professionals and public health experts, as it conflicts with current evidence-based guidelines for COVID-19 prevention and treatment.

Azithromycin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat bacterial infections, while ivermectin is an antiparasitic medication primarily prescribed for conditions such as river blindness and intestinal parasites. Neither drug was originally developed for treating viral infections like COVID-19. Early in the pandemic, both medications were investigated for potential use against COVID-19 due to laboratory studies and anecdotal reports. However, subsequent clinical research and policy reviews have provided important context about their efficacy and safety.

COVID-19 is caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Antibiotics like azithromycin do not treat viral infections; their use is reserved for bacterial co-infections, which are relatively rare in cases of COVID-19. Prescribing antibiotics unnecessarily can contribute to antibiotic resistance, a global health concern. Major health organizations have consistently stated that azithromycin should not be used to prevent or treat COVID-19 unless there is clear evidence of a bacterial infection.

Ivermectin gained attention after preliminary studies suggested it might inhibit the replication of SARS-CoV-2 in laboratory settings. However, large, well-conducted clinical trials have not demonstrated a benefit for ivermectin in preventing or treating COVID-19. Regulatory agencies have emphasized that current evidence does not support its use for COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. There are also safety concerns, as inappropriate dosing or self-medication with ivermectin can lead to serious side effects.

The claim that taking azithromycin and ivermectin during the first three days of symptoms can prevent COVID-19 is not supported by scientific consensus. Prevention of COVID-19 relies primarily on vaccination, physical distancing, mask use in appropriate settings, and good hand hygiene. Early treatment for confirmed COVID-19 cases may include antiviral medications specifically approved for this purpose, but these are prescribed based on individual risk factors and under medical supervision.

Spreading misinformation about unapproved treatments may lead individuals to delay seeking appropriate medical care or to use medications in ways that could be harmful. Medical guidance should be based on the latest scientific evidence and recommendations from qualified healthcare providers. If someone experiences symptoms suggestive of COVID-19, the recommended course of action is to get tested, isolate to prevent transmission, and consult a healthcare professional about appropriate management.

In summary, the claim that azithromycin and ivermectin should be taken to prevent COVID-19 is not supported by current evidence. Individuals are advised to follow established preventive measures and to seek medical advice for treatment decisions, rather than relying on unproven and potentially risky remedies promoted on social media.

Colombian immunologist Manuel Elkin Patarroyo, renowned for his work on malaria vaccines, has made several public statements regarding the COVID-19 pandemic. A recent social media post attributes to Patarroyo claims that the spread of COVID-19 “is not stopped by anyone,” and further suggests that consuming “alkaline” foods, breast milk, antibiotics, aspirin, and bicarbonate can help eliminate or deactivate the virus. These statements have generated significant attention and debate, warranting careful scrutiny and scientific fact-checking.

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, emerged in late 2019 and rapidly became a global health crisis. Scientific understanding of the virus, its transmission, and methods of prevention and treatment have evolved as research continues. Public health authorities worldwide have provided guidelines based on the best available evidence, emphasizing vaccination, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and social distancing as the primary means to prevent and control the spread of the virus.

Analyzing Patarroyo’s alleged statement that COVID-19 “is not stopped by anyone,” it is accurate that, especially early in the pandemic, controlling viral spread was a major challenge. However, this claim ignores the significant impact of coordinated public health measures and vaccination campaigns. Countries that implemented strict containment strategies and achieved high vaccination rates have demonstrated lower infection rates, hospitalizations, and deaths. While it is true that the virus remains endemic and continues to circulate, it is misleading to suggest that no interventions can curb its spread.

The assertion that eating “alkaline” foods can prevent or treat COVID-19 is not supported by scientific evidence. The concept of “alkaline” foods refers to dietary choices that supposedly influence the body's pH level. However, the human body tightly regulates its internal pH regardless of diet. No reputable studies have shown that an “alkaline” diet can prevent viral infections or specifically inhibit SARS-CoV-2.

Regarding breast milk, while it is well established that breast milk provides vital nutrition and antibodies that protect infants from many infections, there is no evidence to suggest that it “eliminates the virus” for COVID-19. Some studies have detected antibodies in the breast milk of mothers who have recovered from COVID-19 or have been vaccinated, which may confer some passive immunity to infants. However, this does not equate to breast milk actively eliminating the virus from the body or serving as a cure.

The claim that antibiotics, aspirin, and bicarbonate can “put the virus out of action” is inaccurate and potentially dangerous. Antibiotics are designed to target bacteria, not viruses, and have no direct effect on SARS-CoV-2. Aspirin is an anti-inflammatory and blood-thinning medication, sometimes used to manage complications in severe cases, but it does not kill the virus. Bicarbonate, commonly known as baking soda, can alter acidity but has no proven antiviral properties against COVID-19. Unsupervised use of these substances can lead to adverse health effects.

In summary, while Manuel Elkin Patarroyo is a respected scientist, the statements attributed to him regarding COVID-19 prevention and treatment do not align with current scientific consensus. Effective control of COVID-19 relies on vaccines and public health measures, not alternative diets or non-specific medications. Public dissemination of unsupported claims risks undermining proven strategies and endangering public health.

A recent social media post claims that the “International Court of Human Rights regulated the use of chlorine dioxide to be administered as medical treatment.” This assertion has generated significant attention and debate online, particularly among communities interested in alternative medical treatments. To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is crucial to examine the relevant international institutions, their authority, and the scientific consensus regarding chlorine dioxide.

First, it is important to clarify that there is no organization officially named the “International Court of Human Rights.” The principal international judicial body associated with human rights is the European Court of Human Rights, which operates under the Council of Europe. Globally, the International Court of Justice settles disputes between states and interprets international law, but it does not regulate medical treatments. Additionally, human rights courts focus on rights violations, not the approval or regulation of pharmaceuticals or medical substances.

Chlorine dioxide is a chemical compound commonly used as an industrial bleach and disinfectant for water treatment. Over recent years, it has been promoted by some groups as a cure or treatment for various ailments, including COVID-19, cancer, and other diseases. However, major health authorities, including the World Health Organization, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration, and the European Medicines Agency, have repeatedly warned against the use of chlorine dioxide for medical purposes. These organizations cite a lack of scientific evidence supporting its efficacy and highlight significant safety risks, such as severe vomiting, diarrhea, and life-threatening low blood pressure due to dehydration.

Contrary to the claim in the social media post, no recognized international legal or health body—including any court—has regulated or approved chlorine dioxide for medical treatment. Regulation of pharmaceuticals and medical substances is typically the responsibility of national or regional health authorities, not international courts. In fact, several countries have specifically banned or cautioned against the sale and use of chlorine dioxide for human consumption.

The proliferation of misinformation regarding chlorine dioxide has prompted regulatory bodies to issue public warnings. The promotion and sale of chlorine dioxide as a medical treatment have led to legal actions in some jurisdictions due to the potential health risks involved. Despite anecdotal reports and online testimonials, the scientific community maintains that chlorine dioxide is not safe or effective as a medical treatment.

In summary, the claim that an “International Court of Human Rights” has regulated chlorine dioxide for medical use is inaccurate. No such court exists with the authority to regulate medical treatments, and chlorine dioxide is not approved by international or national health authorities for use as a medicine. The promotion of chlorine dioxide as a treatment is not supported by scientific evidence and poses significant health risks. Social media users are encouraged to consult reputable sources and rely on guidance from established health authorities when considering medical treatments.

Αυτή η δήλωση έχει προκαλέσει σημαντική προσοχή και διάσκεψη στο διαδίκτυο, ειδικά μεταξύ κοινοτήτων που ενδιαφέρονται για παραλλαγμένες ιατρικές θεραπείες. Για να αξιολογηθεί η ακρίβεια αυτής της δήλωσης, είναι απαραίτητο να εξεταστεί η σχετική διεθνής ιδρυματική δομή, το αξιωματικό της και η επιστημονική συνένταση για το διοξείδιο του χλωρίου.

Πρώτον, είναι σημαντικό να διασαφηνιστεί ότι δεν υπάρχει οργανισμός που να επωνυμίζεται επίσημα ως «Διεθνές Δικαστήριο Ανθρωπίνων Δικαιωμάτων». Το κύριο διεθνές δικαστικό όργανο που σχετίζεται με τα ανθρώπινα δικαιώματα είναι το Ευρωπαϊκό Δικαστήριο των Ανθρωπίνων Δικαιωμάτων, το οποίο λειτουργεί υπό την προϋπόθεση του Συμβουλίου της Ευρώπης. Παγκοσμίως, το Διεθνές Δικαστήριο Ισότητας λύνει συγκρούσεις μεταξύ κρατών και ερμηνεύει το διεθνές δίκαιο, αλλά δεν ρυθμίζει ιατρικές θεραπείες. Επιπλέον, τα δικαστήρια ανθρωπίνων δικαιωμάτων εστιάζουν στις παραβιάσεις δικαιωμάτων, όχι στην έγκριση ή τη ρύθμιση φαρμακευτικών προϊόντων ή ιατρικών ουσιών.

Το διοξείδιο του χλωρίου είναι ένα χημικό συστατικό που χρησιμοποιείται συνήθως ως βλεννοκαθαριστικό και διατροφικό διαλύτης για την επεξεργασία νερού. Αυτό το τελευταίο χρόνο, έχει επικρατήσει η προώθηση από μερικές ομάδες ως θεραπεία ή αποκατάσταση πολλών νοσημάτων, συμπεριλαμβανομένου της νόσου κορονοϊού, του καρκίνου και άλλων ασθενειών. Ωστόσο, μεγάλες αρχές υγείας, συμπεριλαμβανομένου του Οργανισμού Παγκόσμιας Υγείας, της Αμερικανικής Υπηρεσίας Τροφίμων και Φαρμάκων και της Ευρωπαϊκής Αρχής Φαρμάκων, έχουν επανειλημμένα προειδοποιήσει εναντίον της χρήσης του διοξειδίου του χλωρίου για ιατρικούς σκοπούς. Αυτές οι οργανώσεις επισημαίνουν την απουσία επιστημονικών αποδεικτικών δεδομένων για την αποτελεσματικότητά του και υπογραμμίζουν σημαντικά κίνδυνα υγείας, όπως έντονες εμετικές διαταραχές, διαρροία και θανατηφόρα πτώση της αρτηριακής πίεσης λόγω της υποδιατροφής.

Αντίθετα με τη δήλωση του αναρτημένου στα κοινωνικά δίκτυα, καμία αναγνωρισμένη διεθνής νομική ή υγειονομική οργάνωση, συμπεριλαμβανομένων οποιασδήποτε δικαστικής οργάνωσης, έχει ρυθμίσει ή εγκρίνει το διοξείδιο του χλωρίου για ιατρική χρήση. Η ρύθμιση φαρμακευτικών προϊόντων και ιατρικών ουσιών είναι συνήθως της ευθύνης των εθνικών ή περιφερειακών αρχών υγείας, όχι των διεθνών δικαστηρίων. Πράγματι, πολλά κράτη έχουν ειδικά απαγορεύσει ή προειδοποιήσει για την πώληση και τη χρήση του διοξειδίου του χλωρίου για την κατανάλωση ανθρώπων.

Η εκτεταμένη διάδοση της λανθασμένης πληροφόρησης σχετικά με το διοξείδιο του χλωρίου έχει ενθαρρύνει τις αρχές ρύθμισης να εκδώσουν δημόσιες προειδοποιήσεις. Η προώθηση και η πώληση του διοξειδίου του χλωρίου ως ιατρική θεραπεία έχει οδηγήσει σε νομικές διαδικασίες σε μερικές περιοχές λόγω των δυνητικών κινδύνων υγείας που συνδέονται. Αν και υπάρχουν παραδοσιακές αναφορές και αποδείξεις από το διαδίκτυο, η επιστημονική κοινότητα διατηρεί ότι το διοξείδιο του χλωρίου δεν είναι ασφαλές ή αποτελεσματικό ως ιατρική θεραπεία.

Συνοπτικά, η δήλωση ότι το «Διεθνές Δικαστήριο Ανθρωπίνων Δικαιωμάτων» έχει ρυθμίσει το διοξείδιο του χλωρίου για ιατρική χρήση είναι ανακριβής. Δεν υπάρχει τέτοιο δικαστήριο με την αρμοδιότητα να ρυθμίζει ιατρικές θεραπείες, και το διοξείδιο του χλωρίου δεν έχει εγκριθεί από διεθνείς ή εθνικές αρχές υγείας για να χρησιμοποιηθεί ως φαρμακευτικό προϊόν. Η προώθηση του διοξειδίου του χλωρίου ως θεραπεία δεν υποστηρίζεται από επιστημονικά δεδομένα και παρουσιάζει σημαντικούς κινδύνους υγείας. Οι χρήστες των κοινωνικών δικτύων προκαλούν να συμβουλευτούν εξαρτημένες πηγές και να εξαρτηθούν από τις οδηγίες των αναγνωρισμένων αρχών υγείας όταν θα εξετάσουν ιατρικές θεραπείες.

A social media post has recently drawn attention to a website that claims to represent Pfizer and purports to sell COVID-19 vaccines directly to the general public in Mexico. The post raises concerns about the legitimacy of the website, the safety of the products being offered, and the potential for fraud targeting individuals seeking COVID-19 vaccination outside traditional health systems. This fact-checking article investigates the claim, provides background on vaccine distribution, and examines the risks posed by such websites.

**Background and Context**

Pfizer, a global pharmaceutical company, is one of the primary developers of COVID-19 vaccines used worldwide. Since the rollout of its vaccine in late 2020, Pfizer has worked with governments and authorized medical distributors to supply vaccines based on national health regulations. In Mexico, as in most countries, COVID-19 vaccines have been distributed through officially sanctioned government programs, hospitals, and certified pharmacies. Direct-to-consumer sales of COVID-19 vaccines by Pfizer or its authorized partners have not been part of the company’s distribution model.

**Investigating the Website**

Upon review, the website in question uses branding similar to Pfizer’s official website, including logos and imagery commonly associated with the company. However, several red flags arise:

- The website offers COVID-19 vaccines for sale to individuals, bypassing government or medical verification processes.
- Payment methods include untraceable options such as cryptocurrency or wire transfers.
- No clear information is provided about licensing, regulatory compliance, or physical locations in Mexico.
- Contact information is limited or non-functional.

These characteristics are not consistent with legitimate pharmaceutical sales, especially for a regulated product like a COVID-19 vaccine.

**Official Stance on Vaccine Sales**

Pfizer has publicly stated that it does not sell COVID-19 vaccines directly to the public. In Mexico, the federal government has managed vaccine procurement and distribution. Any claims of direct-to-consumer vaccine sales by Pfizer, especially via an online platform, are inconsistent with official policy and established distribution channels.

Health authorities and regulatory agencies in Mexico have repeatedly warned the public about fraudulent websites and scams related to COVID-19 vaccines. These warnings stress that unauthorized sales of vaccines could involve counterfeit, ineffective, or potentially dangerous products.

**Analysis and Conclusion**

Given the evidence, the claim that a website is selling alleged COVID-19 vaccines to the general public in Mexico while presenting itself as Pfizer is highly suspect. The legitimate distribution of COVID-19 vaccines in Mexico does not include direct online sales from the manufacturer to individuals. The website’s lack of transparency, questionable payment methods, and apparent disregard for regulatory requirements strongly suggest it is not an official Pfizer platform.

Members of the public are advised to exercise caution when encountering online offers for vaccines and to rely on government-approved vaccination programs. Purchasing vaccines from unauthorized sources poses significant health and financial risks, including exposure to counterfeit products and personal data theft.

In summary, the core claim of the social media post is accurate in identifying a potentially fraudulent website. There is no evidence that Pfizer sells COVID-19 vaccines directly to the public in Mexico, and the website in question should be regarded with skepticism and reported to authorities.

**زمینه و موقعیت**

پفیزر، شرکت فارماکولوژیک چندملیتی، یکی از اصلی‌ترین توسعه‌کنندگان واکسن کووید-۱۹ در سراسر جهان است. از زمان راه‌اندازی واکسن این شرکت در پایان سال ۲۰۲۰، پفیزر با دولت‌ها و توزیع‌کنندگان پزشکی مجاز همکاری کرده است تا واکسن‌ها را بر اساس قوانین سلامت ملی توزیع کند. در مکزیکو، مانند بسیاری از کشورهای دیگر، واکسن کووید-۱۹ از طریق برنامه‌های دولتی معتبر، بیمارستان‌ها و داروخانه‌های معتبر توزیع شده است. فروش مستقیم واکسن کووید-۱۹ توسط پفیزر یا شرکای مجاز آن به صورت مستقیم به عموم مردم بخشی از مدل توزیع این شرکت نبوده است.

**بررسی سایت مورد نظر**

پس از بررسی، سایت مورد نظر از نظر بranding مشابه سایت رسمی پفیزر استفاده می‌کند، شامل لوگوها و تصاویری که به طور معمول با این شرکت مرتبط هستند. با این حال، چندین علامت قرمز وجود دارد:

- سایت واکسن کووید-۱۹ را به افراد فروش می‌کند، بدون اینکه از فرآیندهای تأیید دولتی یا پزشکی عبور کند.
- روش‌های پرداخت شامل گزینه‌هایی غیرقابل ردیابی مانند رمزارز یا واریز پول به حساب است.
- اطلاعاتی روشن درباره مجوزها، تطابق با مقررات یا محل فیزیکی در مکزیکو ارائه نمی‌شود.
- اطلاعات تماس محدود یا غیرفعال است.

In recent days, social media has circulated alarming claims that authorities in Mexico City have activated a “code blue,” reportedly instructing paramedics to select patients with low chances of survival for palliative care only, deprioritizing life-saving interventions. The post suggests an official policy is in place that directs first responders to withhold full medical efforts from those deemed unlikely to survive, instead focusing resources on patients with better prognoses.

This claim has sparked public concern, with many interpreting it as an indication that the health system is overwhelmed and forced to make difficult triage decisions. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is necessary to understand what “code blue” typically means, the context of emergency response protocols in Mexico City, and whether such a policy is in effect.

**Understanding “Code Blue”**

In medical settings worldwide, the term “code blue” commonly refers to a situation where a patient is in cardiac arrest or requires immediate resuscitation. It is an urgent call for emergency medical teams to respond with all available resources to attempt to save a life. In this context, “code blue” does not imply withholding care but rather the opposite: it is a signal for maximum intervention.

However, during periods of high demand on healthcare systems—such as pandemics or disasters—some regions have implemented protocols for triage, where medical personnel must prioritize patients based on their likelihood of survival. Such protocols, while controversial and emotionally difficult, are sometimes necessary when resources like ventilators or ICU beds are insufficient for the number of critically ill patients.

**Policy in Mexico City**

Mexico City, like many major urban centers, has been challenged by periods of high demand on its health services, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. During the peaks of the pandemic, hospitals faced shortages of beds and staff, leading to triage protocols that prioritized those most likely to benefit from intensive care. However, these protocols were typically enacted within hospital settings, not by paramedics in the field.

There is no official public record or recent announcement from Mexico City’s health authorities about the activation of a city-wide “code blue” policy that instructs paramedics to deny full care to certain patients and only provide palliative care. Standard protocol for paramedics involves assessing the patient’s condition and providing the best possible pre-hospital care, regardless of prognosis, until the patient can be transported to a medical facility unless there are clear signs of death or a do-not-resuscitate order.

**Fact-Checking the Claim**

The social media post misrepresents both the meaning of “code blue” and the current medical protocols in Mexico City. There is no evidence that authorities have activated a policy directing paramedics to systematically deprioritize life-saving care in favor of palliative care for patients with low survival probabilities. While triage decisions are sometimes necessary in overwhelmed systems, they are typically made in hospitals and according to strict ethical guidelines—not as a blanket policy for all paramedics to follow in the field.

**Conclusion**

The core claim of the post—that authorities have enacted a new policy in Mexico City instructing paramedics to withhold care from the gravely ill—is not supported by available information. While resource limitations can impact medical decision-making in crisis situations, there is no evidence of an official “code blue” protocol of this nature currently in effect in Mexico City. Residents should consult official health channels for accurate updates on emergency care protocols.

article_summary: Los medios sociales circulan afirmaciones alarmantes de que autoridades de la Ciudad de México activaron un "código azul" para instruir a paramédicos a priorizar pacientes con mayores probabilidades de supervivencia, desestimando intervenciones de vida o muerte. Sin embargo, el artículo destaca que "código azul" se refiere a emergencias como paro cardíaco, no a la supresión de atención. No existe evidencia de una política oficial en la Ciudad de México que ordene a paramédicos omitir cuidados vitales en favor de cuidados paliativos, ya que los protocolos de triaje se aplican en hospitales, no en el campo.

article_content:
A recent social media post claims, "We do not need a vaccine. We need a body that can resist this and any other virus." This statement reflects a sentiment seen periodically during outbreaks of infectious diseases, including the COVID-19 pandemic, influenza seasons, and other viral threats. The core assertion is that the human body, if sufficiently strong or healthy, could resist all viruses without the need for vaccines. To assess the accuracy and implications of this claim, it is important to examine how the immune system works, the role of vaccines in public health, and the realistic limitations of relying solely on natural immunity.

The human immune system is indeed a powerful defense mechanism. It is composed of innate (non-specific) and adaptive (specific) components that identify and fight against pathogens, including viruses. For many common viral infections, such as the common cold, a healthy immune system often mitigates illness and clears the virus. Lifestyle factors—such as balanced nutrition, regular exercise, adequate sleep, and stress management—can support immune function. However, the fact remains that even healthy individuals can be susceptible to severe complications from certain viruses, such as influenza, measles, polio, or COVID-19.

Relying solely on the body's natural ability to fight viruses overlooks the evolutionary arms race between pathogens and their hosts. Some viruses are highly contagious and capable of causing significant morbidity and mortality, especially among vulnerable groups like infants, the elderly, and those with chronic conditions. There are numerous historical examples where natural immunity alone was insufficient to prevent widespread suffering and death. The global eradication of smallpox, for example, was only possible through mass vaccination, not through natural resistance.

Vaccines work by priming the immune system with components of a virus or bacteria—such as proteins or inactivated forms—so that the body can mount a rapid and effective response if exposed to the real pathogen. This approach avoids the risks associated with acquiring immunity through natural infection, which can result in severe illness or death. Vaccines have also been instrumental in reducing the incidence of many diseases to historically low levels, protecting not only individuals but entire communities through herd immunity.

While it is true that supporting one's immune system through healthy living is beneficial, this alone does not confer resistance to all viruses. Some individuals may have genetic or acquired immune deficiencies, and some viruses are too virulent or novel for the immune system to handle without prior exposure or immunization. The claim that "we do not need a vaccine" disregards decades of evidence showing the effectiveness of vaccines in preventing disease, saving lives, and reducing healthcare burdens.

In summary, the notion that a strong body can resist all viruses without vaccines is not supported by scientific understanding or historical evidence. Both personal health practices and vaccination are important and complementary strategies in preventing and controlling viral infections. Public health experts advocate for vaccination as a proven, safe, and necessary tool to protect individuals and communities, especially against dangerous and highly transmissible viruses.

article_content:
Claims regarding homemade medical devices frequently circulate on social media, particularly in times of public health concern. A recent post suggests that a supplemental or medicinal oxygen tank can be substituted with a handmade “oxygenator” constructed from a nebulizer or a fish tank pump. This claim has garnered attention, especially among individuals seeking cost-effective or accessible alternatives to medically prescribed oxygen therapy. In this article, we examine the validity of this claim and its implications for health and safety.

Medical oxygen therapy is a critical intervention for individuals experiencing respiratory distress or chronic lung conditions such as COPD, pneumonia, or COVID-19. Supplemental oxygen is delivered in carefully controlled concentrations, typically via oxygen tanks, concentrators, or hospital-based systems. These devices are designed to deliver pure or high-concentration oxygen directly to patients, ensuring that their blood oxygen levels remain within a safe range.

The claim centers around the idea that a nebulizer—commonly used to deliver aerosolized medications—or a fish tank pump, which aerates aquarium water, can serve as an improvised oxygen delivery system. The underlying assumption is that these devices can enrich air with sufficient oxygen to support someone with respiratory failure or hypoxemia.

Fact-checking this claim reveals several critical inaccuracies and safety concerns:

1. **Oxygen Concentration**: Medical oxygen tanks and concentrators provide air that is nearly 100% oxygen or, at minimum, significantly higher in oxygen concentration than ambient air (which is about 21% oxygen). Nebulizers and fish tank pumps do not increase the oxygen content of air; they simply move or bubble ambient air, which does not meet the increased oxygen demand of patients in distress.

2. **Device Purpose and Design**: Nebulizers are engineered to turn liquid medication into a mist for inhalation, not to provide supplemental oxygen. Fish tank pumps are designed for aquatic life, not human respiration. Neither device is capable of delivering medical-grade oxygen or maintaining the pressures and flows required for effective oxygen therapy.

3. **Health Risks**: Attempting to substitute prescribed oxygen therapy with a homemade device could lead to severe health consequences. Inadequate oxygen delivery can result in worsening hypoxemia, organ damage, or death. Additionally, improvising with non-medical devices can introduce risks such as contamination, mechanical failure, or unsafe chemical exposure.

4. **Medical Guidance**: Oxygen therapy should only be administered under the supervision of healthcare professionals. The flow and concentration of oxygen must be tailored to the patient’s needs, and improper use of oxygen—even when delivered through proper equipment—can be harmful.

In summary, the claim that a nebulizer or fish tank pump can substitute for a supplemental or medicinal oxygen tank is not supported by medical science or clinical practice. These devices do not increase the concentration of oxygen in the air delivered and are not safe or effective alternatives. Individuals requiring supplemental oxygen should seek medical advice and use only approved medical equipment for their therapy. Relying on homemade “oxygenators” can place individuals at significant risk and is strongly discouraged by medical professionals.

Oxígeno suplementar ta entregad na konsernasion kontroladu, generalmente via tanke di oxígeno, concentradores o sistemas basadu na hospitales. Esos dispositivos ta disenadu pa entregad oxígeno puro o kon konsernasion alta di oxígeno directamente pa pacientes, asegurando ke sù nivel di oxígeno na sangre ta dentro un rango segur.

Esa afirmashon ta basadu na ideya di ke un nebulizador—konveniente pa entregad medicamentos en forma di aerosol—o un bomba di tanke di pez, konveniente pa aerat agua di akvarium, pò servir como un sistema improvisadu pa entregad oxígeno. L'asumishon subyacente ta ke esos dispositivos pò enriqueçer aire kon un nivel suficiente di oxígeno pa sustentad un individuo na falla respiratoriu o hipoxemia.

Verifikashon di fakta di esu afirmashon revela kunsiderable akurasi di konsiderashon y rishos di seguridat:

1. **Konsernasion di Oxígeno**: Tanke di oxígeno médica y concentradores proveen aire ke ta casi 100% oxígeno o, como mínimo, kon un konsernasion di oxígeno significativamente mas alta ke aire ambiente (ke ta alrededor di 21% oxígeno). Nebulizadores y bombas di tanke di pez no aumentan el contenido di oxígeno di aire; ellos simplemente movi o burbuja aire ambiente, ke no satisfaga el demanda aumentadu di oxígeno di pacientes na konsulta.

2. **Propósito y Diseño di Dispositivo**: Nebulizadores ta disenadu pa konvertir un liquido di medicamento en un bruma pa inhalashon, no pa proveer oxígeno suplementar. Bombas di tanke di pez ta disenadu pa vida akuaría, no pa respirashon humana. Ni un dispositivo ta capaz di entregad oxígeno di kalidat médica o mantén presion y flujos nesesarios pa terapi di oxígeno efektiva.

3. **Rishos pa Salud**: Intentando sustituì terapi di oxígeno preskribido kon un dispositivo hech en casa pò lleva a konsiderable konsekuens pa salud. Entregad insuficiente di oxígeno pò resulta en empeoramiento di hipoxemia, daño di órganu o morte. Además, improvisashon kon dispositivos no médicos pò introdusir rishos como kontaminashon, falla mekaniko o expozishon a kímikos insegur.

4. **Güida Médika**: Terapi di oxígeno ta solamente administradu bajo supervishon di profesional di salud. El flujo y konsernasion di oxígeno ta adaptadu pa necesidat di paciente, y usadu inapropiadu di oxígeno—siquiera entregadu via equipamiento aprobadu—pò ser dañino.

En konklusion, esu afirmashon ke un nebulizador o bomba di tanke di pez pò sustituì un tanke di oxígeno suplementar o medicinal no ta apoyadu pa ciensia médica o praxis klinik. Esos dispositivos no aumentan el konsernasion di oxígeno di aire entregadu y no ta alternativas segur o efektivas. Individuos na necesidat di oxígeno suplementar ta debe buscar asesoria médica y usadu solamente equipamiento médico aprobadu pa su terapi. Relianse na "oxigenador" hech en casa pò pòs un risho konsiderable y ta desanadu kuatamente por profesional di salud.
article_summary: Las afirmaciones sobre dispositivos médicos caseros, como "oxigenadores" hechos con nebulizadores o bombas de pecera, circulan en redes sociales durante crisis sanitarias. Estos dispositivos no aumentan la concentración de oxígeno en el aire, lo que los hace ineficaces y peligrosos para tratar distres respiratorio. La falta de control de concentración y flujo de oxígeno puede causar daños graves o incluso la muerte, por lo que se recomienda usar solo equipos médicos aprobados bajo supervisión profesional.

A video circulating widely on social media platforms claims that taking ibuprofen and influenza can fight COVID-19 and even reduce mortality from the disease. The video suggests that this combination provides a protective effect against the coronavirus, leading to confusion and concern among viewers seeking reliable guidance about COVID-19 prevention and treatment. This article examines the validity of this claim and provides context based on current scientific understanding and public health recommendations.

First, it is important to clarify the elements mentioned in the video. Ibuprofen is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) commonly used to reduce pain, fever, and inflammation. “Influenza,” as referenced in the post, is a viral infection caused by the influenza virus, not a medication or supplement. It is unclear from the video whether the claim intends to refer to the influenza infection itself or, perhaps, the influenza vaccine (commonly known as the flu shot). For the purpose of accuracy, both interpretations are considered in this analysis.

Early in the COVID-19 pandemic, there was some public speculation and misinformation regarding the use of ibuprofen. Initial reports suggested that ibuprofen might worsen COVID-19 outcomes, but subsequent reviews and statements from health authorities clarified that there was no conclusive evidence that taking ibuprofen increased the risks associated with COVID-19. In fact, ibuprofen can be used to manage symptoms such as fever and pain in COVID-19 patients, provided there are no other contraindications for its use. However, there is no evidence that ibuprofen “fights” the virus or reduces mortality from COVID-19. Its role is strictly symptomatic relief.

Turning to the claim about influenza, contracting the flu does not protect against COVID-19 and can actually increase the risk of complications, as co-infection with both viruses can strain the immune system and worsen outcomes. If the reference is to the influenza vaccine, it is true that getting a flu shot can help prevent influenza infection, which in turn may reduce the likelihood of simultaneous infection with both viruses. However, the flu vaccine does not directly fight COVID-19 or reduce mortality from it. It is beneficial in preventing influenza, thereby potentially easing the burden on healthcare systems and minimizing the risk of co-infection, but it does not substitute for COVID-19 vaccines or treatments.

The claim that taking ibuprofen and “influenza” can fight COVID-19 and reduce mortality is not supported by scientific evidence. Ibuprofen is useful for managing certain COVID-19 symptoms, but does not treat or cure the infection. Influenza infection should be avoided, not sought, and the influenza vaccine, while important for preventing flu, does not provide direct protection against COVID-19.

In summary, the video’s claim is misleading. The best way to protect against COVID-19 continues to be vaccination, following public health guidelines, and seeking appropriate medical care if infected. Relying on unproven combinations such as ibuprofen and influenza to fight COVID-19 is not recommended by medical authorities and could lead to harmful misunderstandings about disease prevention and treatment.

A viral social media post claims, “In Australia the whole country takes ivermectin,” suggesting that this antiparasitic drug makes people “immune to COVID-19,” and that as a result, “there was not a single infected or a single death” in Australia. This assertion has gained traction online but does not hold up under scrutiny.

**Understanding Ivermectin and Its Approved Uses**

Ivermectin is a medication primarily used to treat parasitic infections in humans and animals. It is approved in many countries, including Australia, for specific conditions such as scabies and certain worm infestations. However, its use as a treatment or preventive measure for COVID-19 has been the subject of considerable debate and research since the beginning of the pandemic.

**Examining the Claim: Did the Whole of Australia Take Ivermectin?**

The claim that “the whole country takes ivermectin” is demonstrably false. Ivermectin has never been officially recommended, mandated, or widely distributed to the entire Australian population as a COVID-19 treatment or preventive. The Australian Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA), the country's regulatory body for medicines, has consistently advised against the use of ivermectin for COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. In fact, as concerns about misuse grew, the TGA restricted the prescription of ivermectin for off-label uses, including COVID-19, in September 2021.

Ivermectin prescriptions did see a slight increase during the pandemic due to misinformation, but uptake was limited and not representative of nationwide adoption.

**Does Ivermectin Make People Immune to COVID-19?**

Scientific evidence does not support the claim that ivermectin provides immunity against COVID-19. While laboratory studies initially suggested possible antiviral effects, subsequent, larger clinical studies did not find clear or consistent benefits of ivermectin in preventing or treating COVID-19. Major health organizations, including those in Australia, caution that there is insufficient evidence to support its use for this purpose.

**Were There No COVID-19 Cases or Deaths in Australia?**

The assertion that there was “not a single infected or a single death” from COVID-19 in Australia is verifiably untrue. Australia, like most countries, experienced multiple waves of COVID-19 infections and deaths. Early in the pandemic, Australia’s strict border controls, quarantine policies, testing, and public health interventions kept case numbers lower than many other countries, but they did not eliminate the virus entirely.

As of mid-2024, Australia has reported millions of COVID-19 cases and tens of thousands of deaths. These numbers reflect a substantial public health impact, despite the country’s initial success in containing outbreaks.

**Conclusion**

The social media post’s core claims—that the entire population of Australia took ivermectin, that the drug makes people immune to COVID-19, and that Australia saw no COVID-19 cases or deaths—are all false. Ivermectin is not approved or recommended for COVID-19 prevention or treatment in Australia, and the country has experienced significant COVID-19 cases and fatalities. Public health experts urge reliance on proven interventions, such as vaccination, masking, and social distancing, rather than unproven treatments.

**了解伊维菌素及其获批用途**

伊维菌素是一种主要用于治疗人类和动物寄生虫感染的药物。在包括澳大利亚在内的许多国家，该药物被批准用于治疗特定疾病，如疥疮和某些蠕虫感染。然而，自疫情开始以来，其作为新冠病毒治疗或预防药物的用途一直备受争议，并成为研究的焦点。

**审视这一说法：澳大利亚全民都服用了伊维菌素吗？**

“整个国家都服用了伊维菌素”这一说法显然是错误的。伊维菌素从未被官方推荐、强制或广泛分发给澳大利亚全体人口作为新冠病毒的治疗或预防手段。澳大利亚药品监管机构澳大利亚治疗用品管理局（TGA）始终建议，除临床试验外，不应将伊维菌素用于新冠病毒的治疗。事实上，随着对滥用的担忧加剧，TGA于2021年9月限制了伊维菌素用于非标用途（包括新冠病毒）的处方。

尽管疫情期间存在误导性信息，伊维菌素的处方数量有所上升，但实际使用范围有限，不能代表全国范围内的普及。

**伊维菌素能让人们免受新冠病毒感染吗？**

科学证据并不支持伊维菌素能提供对新冠病毒的免疫力。虽然早期实验室研究显示可能具有抗病毒效果，但后续更大规模的临床研究并未发现伊维菌素在预防或治疗新冠病毒方面具有明确或一致的益处。包括澳大利亚在内的主要卫生组织都警告称，目前尚无足够证据支持其用于此目的。

**澳大利亚真的没有新冠病毒感染或死亡病例吗？**

“澳大利亚没有一例感染或一例死亡”这一说法明显不实。澳大利亚和其他大多数国家一样，经历了多轮新冠病毒感染和死亡。疫情初期，澳大利亚严格的边境管控、检疫政策、检测和公共卫生措施使病例数低于许多其他国家，但并未彻底消除病毒。

截至2024年中期，澳大利亚已报告数百万例新冠病毒感染病例和数万例死亡。这些数据反映了重大的公共卫生影响，尽管该国在疫情初期成功遏制了疫情爆发。

**结论**

该社交媒体帖子的核心说法——澳大利亚全民都服用了伊维菌素、该药物能让人对新冠病毒免疫、澳大利亚没有新冠病毒感染或死亡病例——均不属实。伊维菌素在澳大利亚未被批准或推荐用于新冠病毒的预防或治疗，而该国经历了大量新冠病毒感染和死亡病例。公共卫生专家敦促依赖经过验证的干预措施，如疫苗接种、佩戴口罩和保持社交距离，而非未经证实的治疗方法。

article_content:
A recent social media post has claimed that the AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine contains “genetically modified embryonic human kidney cells” and suggests that these cells can be sourced from human embryos “reared in test tubes.” This statement has elicited concern and confusion among the public regarding the vaccine’s composition and the methods used in its development. Here, we break down the claim and analyze its accuracy, providing clear context and factual information.

To start, it is important to understand the role of human cell lines in vaccine development. The AstraZeneca vaccine, also known as Vaxzevria or Covishield in some regions, utilizes a harmless adenovirus vector to deliver genetic instructions for the body to produce a portion of the coronavirus spike protein, triggering an immune response. In the manufacturing process, the vaccine’s viral vector is initially grown in a type of human cell line known as HEK-293.

HEK-293 stands for “Human Embryonic Kidney 293.” This cell line was originally derived in the early 1970s from the kidney cells of a single human fetus that was legally aborted. The cells were then modified and adapted to grow in laboratory conditions. Over the decades, these cells have been cultured and replicated millions of times and are now a staple in biological and medical research. Importantly, HEK-293 cells used today are not directly harvested from new embryos but are descendants of the original cell line, propagated in laboratories.

The claim that the AstraZeneca vaccine “contains” these human cells is misleading. While the vaccine’s viral vector is produced using HEK-293 cells, the manufacturing process includes purification steps to remove the cells themselves from the final product. Trace amounts of residual proteins or DNA fragments from the HEK-293 cells may remain, but the vaccine does not contain whole, living human cells. Regulatory agencies monitor these residuals to ensure they are present only at extremely low, safe levels.

Furthermore, the statement that these cells can be obtained from “human embryos reared in test tubes” is not accurate. The HEK-293 cell line was derived from a single fetal kidney sample decades ago and is continuously cultured in laboratories; there is no ongoing need to obtain new embryonic tissue for this purpose. The phrase “reared in test tubes” misrepresents the scientific process and may evoke a misleading image of how these cells are sourced.

In summary, the AstraZeneca vaccine does not contain genetically modified embryonic human kidney cells, though it is produced using a laboratory-grown cell line originally derived from fetal tissue over 50 years ago. No new embryos are used in the vaccine’s production, and the final vaccine product does not include whole human cells. While trace genetic material from these cells may be present, it is rigorously regulated and considered safe by health authorities. Understanding these scientific details helps clarify misconceptions and supports informed decisions about vaccination.
